title: JWST Observations of Starbursts: Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons in the NGC 253 Superwind
authors: Serena A. Cronin, Alberto D. Bolatto, Rebecca C. Levy, Karl D. Gordon, Elizabeth Tarantino, Martha L. Boyer, Lindsey Hands, Hannah B. Koziol, Adam K. Leroy, Patricia A. Arens, Leindert A. Boogaard, Daniel A. Dale, Fergus R. Donnan, Grant P. Donnelly, Kimberly L. Emig, Deanne B. Fisher, Rodrigo Herrera-Camus, Ralf S. Klessen, Thomas S.-Y. Lai, Laura Lenkić, Ashley E. Lieber, Laura A. Lopez, Sebastian Lopez, David S. Meier, Elisabeth A.C. Mills, Juergen Ott, Debosmita Pathak, Sophie L. Robbins, Helena M. Richie, Karin M. Sandstrom, Kaitlyn E. Sheriff, J.D.T. Smith, Yu-Hsuan Teng, Sylvain Veilleux, Vicente Villanueva, Fabian Walter, Paul P. van der Werf
abstract: We present the first spatially resolved study of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) evolution in the galactic superwind of the nearby (d~3.5Mpc) galaxy NGC 253. Using JWST MIRI and NIRCam, we image ~$\pm$2kpc along the galaxy minor axis, capturing both sides of the starburst-driven wind at ~0.05''-0.375'' (~0.85-6.4pc) resolution and providing one of the most detailed views of the wind to date. We target PAH emission at 3.3um, 7.7um, and 11.3um, revealing PAH-bright filamentary streamers along the limb-brightened edges of the outflow cones out to at least a deprojected distance r~0.5kpc, beyond which they likely become confused with the spiral arms. In the southwest (SW) and northeast (NE) streamers, PAH intensity declines faster than $r^{-2}$, suggesting either PAH destruction or a decrease in gas column density or dust-to-gas ratio rather than a response to declining illumination alone. Band ratios trace changes in PAH properties, with the 11.3/7.7um ratio increasing with distance in the SW and northwest (NW) streamers and 3.3/7.7um and 3.3/11.3um decreasing in the SW and NE streamers, indicating larger, more neutral PAHs farther from the starburst. Given the thermal and dynamical properties of the gas in the SW streamer, cool gas is expected to survive acceleration in the outflow and enable PAH shielding. Compared with those of the prototypical starburst M82, the NGC 253 band ratios indicate faster evolution in PAH size. Thus, the NGC 253 wind may represent an earlier stage of outflow evolution in which small PAHs are destroyed near the starburst within the first few Myr.
comments: 18 pages, 5 main figures, 4 appendix figures, submitted to ApJL

figs.cap: JWST imaging along the minor axis of NGC 253 out to $\sim\pm 2$ kpc and on $\sim 0.85{-}6.4$ pc scales. (Left) Multi-color MIRI image using the filters F560W (cyan; continuum and some PAHs at $6.2~\mu$m), F770W (orange; PAHs at $7.7~\micron$ and some continuum), and F1130W (red; PAHs at $11.3~\micron$ and some continuum). The limb-brightened edges of the outflow cone are evident, with wispy sub-structure in all four streamers. The northern wind is seen through the disk while the southern wind is pointed toward the observer and in front of the disk. (Right) Composite NIRCam imaging using the following filters: F140M and F164N (blue; continuum and [Fe II]), F212N and F250M (green; H$_{2}$ and continuum), and F335M and F360M (red; PAHs at $3.3~\micron$ plus continuum). The $3.3~\micron$ PAH complex is brightest in the spiral arms and bar; the fainter wind is hidden by the bright stellar disk. Image processing by A. Pagan (STScI).

Emission maps of the $3.3~\micron$, $7.7~\micron$, and $11.3~\micron$ PAH features in the central $2\times 2$ kpc region of NGC 253. The $3.3~\micron$ map is continuum-subtracted from F335M using two flanking filters (F250M and F360M), while the $7.7~\micron$ and $11.3~\micron$ maps are both background- and continuum-subtracted. The continuum images at all three wavelengths are in Figure 6 of the Appendix. Labeled dashed rectangles mark the four wind streamers where we extract measurements (zoom-ins in the bottom row to show detailed sub-structure). Unlabeled dotted rectangles mark the adjacent off-streamer regions used to estimate disk-only PAH emission, since the disk contributes to each line of sight.

Binned-mean emission profiles extracted along each NGC 253 streamer (colored points) with M82 (gray points) and arbitrary $r^{-2}$ and $r^{-3}$ profiles for comparison. The shaded regions are the standard error of the mean. Each profile is multiplied by $r^{2}$ to divide out the geometric dilution expected for illumination by the starburst, so that a flat ($r^{-2}$) profile indicates changes in PAH emission due to distance from the starburst. The top $x{-}$axis converts the deprojected distance to a timescale assuming a cool-outflow speed of $200$ km s$^{-1}$. All PAH bands in the SW and NE streamers decline faster than $r^{-2}$, suggesting possible changes to PAH emission that are not due to distance from the illuminating starburst. The NW streamer roughly follows $\sim r^{-2}$ much like M82. We exclude the SE streamer, where we do not produce a reliable disk subtraction.

PAH ratios along each NGC 253 streamer, computed from the emission profiles in Figure 3, with the M82 ratios for comparison [29, gray;]. Ratios are intensity-weighted so that fainter regions do not skew them. We divide $11.3/7.7~\micron$ by 20 for display, and the $x{-}$axes are deprojected distance from the starburst nucleus and the timescale over that distance assuming $v\sim 200$ km s$^{-1}$. The SW streamer shows clear trends of the $11.3/7.7~\micron$ ratio increasing with distance, as in M82, and the $3.3/7.7~\micron$ and $3.3/11.3~\micron$ ratios decreasing, unlike the roughly flat ratios of M82. Beyond ${\sim}0.2{-}0.3$ kpc, $11.3/7.7~\micron$ in the NE and NW agrees with M82. The $3.3~\micron$ ratios vary from streamer to streamer and do not follow M82’s flat profiles.

Ratios from Figure 4 compared with continuum-subtracted Draine et al. [34] dust models, assuming a $3{-}10$ Myr starburst at solar metallicity [18]. Each grid corresponds to a radiation field intensity $U$ at $A_{\rm V}=0$. The small black arrow shows the magnitude and direction of how the grids shift for a higher extinction of $A_{\rm V}=5$, and the long black arrows show the effects of PAH size and ionization. Points are colored by distance from the nucleus. The gray arrow shows the M82 trend from $0.3$ kpc (excluding inner points affected by silicate absorption) to $0.6$ kpc (the most extended NGC 253 streamer). White symbols show median PHANGS-JWST ratios across galaxies [85] for star-forming disks, disk-like galaxy centers (“disky center”), and young star-forming centers or central molecular zones (CMZs). Silicate absorption affecting the $11.3~\micron$ feature near the starburst may explain some ratios outside the $A_{\rm V}=0$ grids. In the SW streamer, PAHs become larger and more neutral with distance, matching M82 but spanning a wider range over the same distance and timescale. NGC 253 ratios fall near the PHANGS-JWST medians, with the outermost SW and NE ratios matching disks and disk-like centers, and the innermost ratios matching CMZs. Figure 8 shows the NGC 253 ratios without disk subtraction.

(Left) Estimated continuum in the F335M filter as a result of the continuum-subtraction process in Section II. The continuum appears dominated by starlight with no visible outflow emission. (Middle, Right) Estimated percentage of continuum contributing to the F770W and F1130W filters after using the approach from L. Hands et al. (in prep). In the outflow, the median continuum contribution to F770W and F1130W is $\sim 20\%$.

title: Seeing through the fog: astrophysical priors and the evidence for new physics in pulsar timing arrays
authors: Torsten Bringmann, Chris Gordon, Carlo Tasillo
abstract: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) have found evidence for a gravitational wave background at nHz frequencies. Inspiralling supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) likely contribute to at least part of the signal, but there may be additional cosmological sources from new physics in the early universe. Disentangling the two is complicated by the prohibitively slow modelling of SMBHB spectra based on realistic population models. Here we introduce binaryfog, a surrogate of up-to-date population models also used by the NANOGrav collaboration, that returns the statistical distribution of bent spectra $\mathcal{O}(10^6)$ faster than direct computation. We use binaryfog to profile over the six astrophysical parameters in fits of four extensively discussed new-physics models: a dark sector phase transition, cosmic superstrings, inflationary gravitational waves, and domain walls. Compared to the widely adopted power-law description of the SMBHB background, the preference for a phase transition drops from $2.8\sigma$ to $1.5\sigma$. The other three models follow a similar pattern. We also recommend updated astrophysical priors based on galaxy surveys published since 2014, which for current PTA data still only give a marginal preference of $1.7\sigma$ for a phase transition. An interpretation of the signal in terms of SMBHBs alone favours binaries that merge within about $2\,$Gyr after their host galaxies have merged, requiring an efficient mechanism to overcome the final parsec of separation. If binaries need longer than about $6.5\,$Gyr to merge, the preference for a phase transition exceeds $3\sigma$ under our recommended updated prior set. binaryfog can help resolve these questions, as it allows users to study the impact of updated astrophysical priors and a realistic SMBHB population model on new-physics searches with PTAs.
comments: 42 pages, 9 figures

figs.cap: The median predicted SMBHB spectra that result when individually varying each of the six parameters of the population model (left) and, alternatively, the two parameters of the $(A,\gamma)$ power law (right) across the indicated range (the $2\sigma$ range of the NANOGrav priors for the four Gaussian parameters, and the full range of the uniform priors for $\tau_{\mathrm{f}}$ and $\nu_{\mathrm{inner}}$, cf. table 1). We restrict ourselves to $m_{\psi,0}>10.5$ here since the $2\sigma$ range of the NANOGrav prior reaches below the lower limit of the uniform prior used to generate the model library. The five values in each panel are equally spaced, dark blue for the smallest and yellow for the largest, with the other parameters at the centres of the NANOGrav priors; for the power law the range is the centre of its Gaussian prior $\pm 2\sigma$. For comparison, we also show our baseline free spectrum, the CURN spectrum of the 2026 NANOGrav 15 yr release [48].

The gravitational wave background of the binaries predicted under the NANOGrav (left), Tomczak–Kormendy (middle) and survey-average priors (right) of table 1, before any fit to the timing data, from binaryfog with $40000$ draws from each prior set and one realisation of the background per draw. Solid lines show the median, shaded bands the $1\sigma$ range over the prior and the realisation scatter. The dashed lines show the $1\sigma$ range due to the remaining four astrophysical parameters and realisation scatter when $\tau_{\mathrm{f}}$ and $\nu_{\mathrm{inner}}$ are held fixed. This range is averaged over their uniform priors and centred on the median of the full distribution. For the Tomczak–Kormendy and survey-average priors these two hardening parameters set most of the width of the band. The violins are the NANOGrav 15 yr CURN free spectrum. Under all three prior sets the median prediction lies below the measured spectrum, in the lowest bin by $0.8\,$dex in $h^{2}\Omega_{\mathrm{GW}}$ for the NANOGrav and Tomczak–Kormendy priors and by $0.2\,$dex for the survey-average priors.

(7) with the skew $c=0.22$ of the surrogate at this point (orange, solid) and the map-Airy distribution (dark blue, dash-dotted), each matched to the same median and width. The spike of the warp is the probability it piles up at its floor (section 2.2). Middle panel: The posterior of the amplitude of the bin in the NANOGrav CURN free spectrum, as a function of the binary amplitude. Bottom panel: The product of the two top panels, the integrand of eq. (12), normalised such that the area under the histogram equals one. The annotated numbers denote $\Delta\ln L$, the difference of the logarithm of the area under the histogram and the respective parametrisation of the same colour, corresponding to the difference in the likelihood when using the respective distributions. The warp of eq. (7) is the only one which consistently reproduces the likelihood of the realisations on the (sub-)per cent level across the bins.

Posteriors for the six astrophysical parameters obtained with binaryfog (thick) against those extracted from the vector graphics of figure 9 of refs. [8, 48] (thin), for flat priors over the ranges in table 1 (blue) and the NANOGrav priors (orange). Our fits in this figure and the published ones both use the 2026 HD+MP+DP+CURN free spectrum. The published contours derive from an unsmoothed histogram of 34 bins; pieces spanning fewer than three bins are not drawn here. Contours enclose the $1$, $2$, and $3\sigma$ credible regions; the diagonal shows the one-dimensional marginalised posteriors.

Left panel: The allowed region in the plane of phase transition strength $\alpha$ and inverse duration $\beta/H$, with $T_{\mathrm{reh}}$ being profiled over. With the binaries treated as a population with realisation scatter under the NANOGrav priors (orange), the preferred regions are significantly larger than with the commonly adopted $(A,\gamma)$ power law [21] (dashed blue) as well as with no binaries included in the fit (dotted blue); in all cases, darker (lighter) colours refer to $1\sigma$ ($2\sigma$) confidence regions. The symbols mark the best fit of each treatment, whose spectrum is shown on the right; the maxima lie on a ridge along which $\ln L$ changes by less than $10^{-4}$. The binaryfog $2\sigma$ region covers the whole panel outside the hatched region, in which the gravitational waves of the phase transition alone add more than $0.22$ to $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ [102]. Right panel: The best-fit spectra for a phase transition alone, a phase transition combined with the $(A,\gamma)$ power-law background, and a phase transition combined with the binaryfog population model, compared with the NANOGrav 15 yr CURN spectrum. Also shown is the best fit of the binaries alone (green), with the band containing 90% of its realisations.

Comparison of the impact of a population-based astrophysical background instead of a power law on the preferred parameter regions for three distinct new-physics models. The solid curves in the top panels indicate the total signal for a given model parameter as marked by a triangle in the lower panels; their dashed and dotted counterparts indicate the astrophysical and the new-physics contributions, with the shaded bands holding 90% of the realisations the respective population would produce. Magenta curves belong to the best fit, purple (green) curves to the lower (upper) end of the $2\sigma$-favoured region in parameter space; these are the ends and the best fit of the binaryfog interval. In the lower panels, we plot the profile likelihood ratio, with the dotted horizontal lines indicating the $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ thresholds. The shaded bands represent the $2\sigma$ intervals resulting from the NANOGrav 15 yr common uncorrelated red noise spectrum, when using the power-law (light blue) or binaryfog prescription (orange) for the SMBHB contribution, respectively.

title: Gaia's promise to detect compact-object binaries II: Predictions for dormant neutron star binaries in DR4 and beyond
authors: Chirag Chawla, Sourav Chatterjee, Katelyn Breivik
abstract: With the fourth data release (DR4) from Gaia imminent, we predict neutron star (NS) binaries with luminous companions (LCs) expected to be detectable in DR4 and the final data release (DR5). We create realistic synthetic populations of NS--LC binaries in the Milky Way using COSMIC, assuming (a) observationally motivated initial distributions of binary properties, (b) metallicity and location dependent star formation history of the MW adopted from the FIRE-2 galaxy m12i, and (c) all relevant binary interaction physics, with the rapid and delayed supernova prescriptions. We estimate the detectable NS--LC population using an approximate Gaia\ selection function based on projected orbital size of the LC as well as gaiamock, which emulates Gaia's multi-epoch astrometry and orbit-fitting pipeline- both after taking into account extinction and reddening. Across supernova models and statistical fluctuations, the former (gaiamock) pipeline predicts $\sim14$--$29$ ($\sim1$--$8$), $4500$--$4700$ ($100$--$110$), and $4800$--$5000$ ($300$--$380$) detectable NS--LC binaries in DR3, DR4, and DR5, respectively. While the orbital-size based pipeline brackets the DR3 yield of NS--LC candidates, the gaiamock prediction falls short, suggesting uncertainties in the modeled binary evolution or contributions from other formation channels. DR4 is expected to directly shed light on the the relative importance of detectable NS--LC binaries from isolated binary evolution vis a vis other channels such as dynamical formation. Interestingly, our models suggest that future releases will also include $22^{+7}_{-5}\ (13^{+5}_{-4})$ and $124^{+14}_{-15}\ (53^{+10}_{-6})$ gaiamock-detectable pulsar--MS binaries in DR4 and DR5, respectively, for the rapid (delayed) model, which are prime targets for radio follow-up.
comments: 28 pages, 13 figures, 1 table, submitted to the Astrophysical Journal; comments welcome

title: Fast X-ray Transients as Premature-Dissipated Gamma-Ray Bursts with Magnetic-Dominated Jets
authors: Shu-Xu Yi, Shao-Lin Xiong
abstract: Fast X-ray transients (FXTs) are extragalactic X-ray flashes with little or no accompanying $\gamma$-ray emission. We propose that FXTs and classical gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) share a common origin in Poynting-flux-dominated jets powered by the Blandford--Znajek mechanism. In this picture, FXTs arise when the kink instability triggers premature dissipation at small radii ($\sim 10^{11}$~cm), yielding low Lorentz factors ($\Gamma \lesssim 50$) and high compactness ($\ell' \gg 1$) that thermalize the emission into the soft X-ray band. When the kink criterion is not met, the jet accelerates to ultra-relativistic velocities ($\Gamma > 100$) and dissipates at larger radii ($\sim 10^{15}$~cm) as a standard GRB. This scenario can naturally explain the observed thermal spectra, low $E_{\rm peak}$, supernova associations, jet-break absence, and day-scale afterglow delays across five well-studied FXTs. EP240801a is explained as a boundary event, where premature dissipation does not exhaust the full magnetic energy; the residual energy is further dissipated at a typical GRB radius, producing the observed $\gamma$-ray prompt emission with an $\sim 80$~s time lag. A key observational prediction is that FXTs may exhibit $e^+ e^-$ annihilation line features sweeping from a few MeV to hundreds of keV within $\sim 0.01$~s.
comments: 7 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJL

figs.cap: Schematic of the jet evolution scenario. A Poynting-flux-dominated jet is launched from the central engine and propagates through the progenitor envelope. Kink instability may develops in the magnetically dominated flow, triggering premature magnetic dissipation at low Lorentz factor, producing the fast X-ray transient (FXT). In the sketch, we also plot the case when the premature dissipation is absence, the jet continues accelerating to ultra-relativistic Lorentz factor and produces a classical gamma-ray burst (GRB) via dissipation at larger radii.

Model prediction for $\Gamma(R_{\rm dis})$ (solid black, left axis) and $\ell^{\prime}$ (dashed, right axis, for $L=10^{48}$ erg s$^{-1}$) as functions of $\sigma_{0}$. Red shading: FXT regime ($\sigma_{0}<45$, premature dissipation at $R_{*}$). Blue shading: GRB regime ($\sigma_{0}>45$, dissipation beyond $R_{*}$). The vertical segment at $\sigma_{0}=45$ connects the two branches. Observed events are marked at their inferred $\sigma_{0}$: EP241113a ($\Gamma\approx 20$; Dai et al. 2026) and EP240414a ($\Gamma\approx 6.5$, from the inner cocoon constraint of Zheng et al. 2025) have $\Gamma$ measurements in the literature; events marked with $^{∗}$ (EP250108a, XRF 241001A) lack a precise $\Gamma$ measurement and are shown at illustrative $\sigma_{0}$ values. EP240801a$^{∗}$ is placed at the FXT/GRB boundary ($\sigma_{0}=45$) by model construction; its $\Gamma$ is not independently constrained by observations.

title: Isotropic diffuse gamma-ray flux limits from Carpet-3 experiment data using neural networks with domain adaptation
authors: D. D. Dzhappuev, I. M. Dzaparova, T. A. Dzhatdoev, E. A. Gorbacheva, I. S. Karpikov, M. M. Khadzhiev, A. U. Kudzhaev, A. N. Kurenya, A. S. Lidvansky, O. I. Mikhailova, V. B. Petkov, N. A. Pozdnukhov, V. S. Romanenko, G. I. Rubtsov, S. V. Troitsky, I. B. Unatlokov, N. A. Vasiliev, A. F. Yanin, K. V. Zhuravleva
abstract: Diffuse gamma rays above 100 TeV probe PeV cosmic rays and astrophysical neutrino sources. Their strong attenuation on background radiation makes the observed flux sensitive to the location of the emission and to possible modifications of photon propagation. Searches for an isotropic component require rejection of an overwhelming hadronic background, but uncertainties in air-shower physics, cosmic-ray composition and detector response can lead to differences between simulated and measured events. Here we report upper limits on the isotropic diffuse gamma-ray flux from 100 TeV to 10 PeV using 1078 days of Carpet-3 observations collected between 2022 and 2026. We identify photon candidates with a neural network combining the surface-array signals and measurements from the upgraded 410 $\mathrm{m^2}$ muon detector. Unsupervised domain adaptation uses unlabeled experimental events during training to mitigate the impact of simulation--data discrepancies on the classification. The limits are among the strongest available and provide benchmarks for tests of extended Galactic emission and modified photon propagation from extragalactic sources.
comments: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables

title: Are AGN Required? Updated Photoionization Models for Rest-UV Line Diagnostics in Reionization-era Galaxies
authors: Jiayang Yang, Casey Papovich, Weida Hu, Taylor A. Hutchison, Rebecca L. Larson, Pablo Arrabal Haro, Anthony J. Taylor, Ray Garner III, Kaila Ronayne, Nikko J. Cleri, Steven L. Finkelstein, Bren E. Backhaus, Micaela B. Bagley, Justin W. Cole, Jeyhan S. Kartaltepe
abstract: Rest-frame ultraviolet (UV) emission lines in galaxies provide important probes of the ionizing radiation, chemical abundances, and interstellar medium conditions. Here, we consider UV emission-line diagnostics for galaxies with the observed physical properties of young, metal-poor stellar populations in the epoch of reionization. We study eight $z \sim 7$--$9$ galaxies using deep JWST/NIRSpec G140M and G395M spectroscopy from the Carbon-3 plus Oxygen survey. We measure rest-frame UV and optical emission lines, $\mathrm{C\,IV}$ $\lambda\lambda1548,1551$, $\mathrm{He\,II}$ $\lambda1640$, $\mathrm{O\,III]}$ $\lambda1666$, $\mathrm{C\,III]}$ $\lambda\lambda1907,1909$, $\mathrm{[O\,II]}$ $\lambda\lambda3727,3730$, H$\gamma$, $\mathrm{[O\,III]}$ $\lambda4364$, H$\beta$, and $\mathrm{[O\,III]}$ $\lambda\lambda4960,5008$. The galaxies have low oxygen abundances, $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=7.50$-$7.90$, low C/O ratios, $\mathrm{C/O}=0.10$-$0.32$, and high electron densities, $n_e(\mathrm{C\,III]})=(1.9-4.9)\times10^4\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$. We compute Cloudy photoionization models using BPASS and BC03 stellar populations to test how lower C/O and higher gas density affect the UV diagnostics. We find that reducing C/O and increasing the gas density shift the star-forming grids into regions conventionally classified as composite or AGN-like. We therefore conclude that positions within these regions alone do not establish the presence of an AGN in the galaxies studied here. However, some lines remain enigmatic, including strong $\mathrm{He\,II}$, which is not reproduced by the updated models. These results highlight the need for UV diagnostic boundaries that account for the abundance patterns and gas conditions of galaxies during the epoch of reionization.

title: Lunar laser ranging analyses of NGLR-1 data with PEP and prospects for MPAc: towards one millimeter range precision
authors: G. Bargiacchi, J. Chandler, N. Burzillà, R. Campagnola, L.Porcelli, D. Currie, J.D. Carpenter, N. Boersma, L. Cacciapuoti, P. Firme, P. Ruzza, I. Lebouteiller, C. Courde, J. Chabé, J. Eckl, S. Merkowitz, N. Colmenares, R. Reasenberg, I. Shapiro, S. Dell'Agnello
abstract: Since 1969, Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) has provided critical data for investigating Earth-Moon dynamics, lunar internal structure, and tests of General Relativity (GR). However, the measurement precision of historical arrays (such as those from Apollo and Lunokhod missions) is inherently limited by laser pulse broadening induced by lunar librations. To overcome this limit, next-generation single Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs) of large optical diameter have been developed to eliminate pulse dispersion, enabling LLR measurements to advance from centimeter-level precision down to the millimeter scale. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of LLR observations from NGLR-1 (Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1), the first single 10cm-diameter CCR deployed on the lunar surface. Carried out using the Planetary Ephemeris Program (PEP), this study investigates individual range measurements, normal points (NPs), residuals, and observational dispersion collected by the ground stations at Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging station (APOL), Wettzell, and Grasse. The results: demonstrate the success of NGLR-1 in significantly enhancing time of flight measurement precision compared to legacy Apollo and Lunokhod retroreflector arrays; indicate similar good prospects also for ESA's MPAc laser retroreflector (MoonLIGHT with Pointing Actuators) to be launched in early 2027; pave the way for a new era of LLR observations and enhanced tests of GR, alternative gravity theories in general and improved lunar geophysics and geodesy.

title: Orbital parameters for 50 million stars observed by Gaia and spectroscopic surveys
authors: Nayara I. Feliciano-Souza, Hélio D. Perottoni, Diogo Souto, Friedrich Anders, João A. S. Amarante, Guilherme Limberg, Chloé Padois, Rafael M. Santucci, Teresa Antoja, Helio J. Rocha Pinto, Eder Martioli, Arman Khalatyan
abstract: Together with ground-based spectroscopic stellar surveys, the Gaia mission has changed Galactic archaeology over the past decade. Nevertheless, attempts to combine these datasets remain scarce, even though precise orbital parameters for as many stars as possible are crucial to unraveling the Galaxy's formation and evolutionary history. This work aims to construct the largest homogeneous catalog of stellar orbital parameters ever compiled to date, using the most up-to-date data from nine large-scale spectroscopic stellar surveys (Gaia RVS DR3, APOGEE DR19, BOSS DR19, LAMOST DR11, Gaia-ESO DR5, GALAH DR4, RAVE DR6, SEGUE DR12, DESI DR1), combined with Gaia DR3 astrometric data and employing an orbital integration tool for orbital modeling. Our catalog includes orbital parameters, such as orbital distances, eccentricity, inclination, energy, angular momentum, and actions, for 52,423,233 stellar sources from Bailer-Jones distances, and 40,355,569 stellar sources from recomputed StarHorse distances, of which 41,100,866 and 30,777,133 are unique objects, respectively. We also included probabilities of belonging to specific Galactic components based on kinematic classification and chemical-abundance classification. Using this catalog, we recover the known kinematic substructures of the Galactic disk while extending their mapping to Galactocentric distances of $\sim17$ kpc, demonstrating the potential of the combined dataset for studies of Galactic dynamics and evolution. We expect that this catalog will benefit a broad range of research areas, from stellar astrophysics to Galactic archaeology.

title: Mining the time axis with TRON. IV. MeerKAT detects a radio burst from a nearby M~dwarf
authors: A. J. T. Ramaila, O. M. Smirnov, T. Myburgh, D. A. H. Buckley, O. D. Egbo, I. Monageng, A. Golden, D. N'i Chonchubhair, X. Mao, M. A. Thompson, B. Ngcebetsha, C. Tasse, I. Heywood, J. S. Kenyon, S. J. Perkins, J. Dawson, H. L. Bester, J. S. Bright, T. Blecher, N. Oozeer, V. G. G. Samboco, I. Sihlangu, C. Choza
abstract: We report the detection of a minute-timescale, highly circularly polarised ($\sim100\%$) radio burst from an active M dwarf (spectral type M1Ve), PM J14111$-$6155, located 19.6 pc from the Sun. Identified in the 1.28 GHz SMGPS using 8-second integrations from the TRON-pipeline, the burst peaked at 7.7 mJy. Visibility-based dynamic spectra reveal a drifting, band-limited emission feature ($\sim$300 MHz FWHM) with a maximum cut-off near 1.65 GHz, associated with electron cyclotron maser instability (ECMI), implying the existence of large-scale magnetic topologies ($B_* \approx 0.59$ kG). A non-detection ($3\sigma$ upper limit) four hours later points to intermittent or rotationally modulated beamed emission. An analysis of both TESS and ground-based survey data failed to recover an unambiguous rotational period for the optical counterpart. Follow-up SALT spectroscopy confirms its active chromospheric state, exhibiting prominent emission in the Ca {\sc ii} infrared triplet, Balmer lines, and persistent double-peaked H$\alpha$ emission ($44.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ peak separation) attributable to optically thick self-absorption. This discovery demonstrates that the coordinated use of time-series optical photometry, high-resolution spectroscopy, and high-cadence spectropolarimetric radio imaging enables direct probing of coherent radio emission from the magnetically active atmospheres of nearby M dwarfs.
comments: 7 pages, 6 figures, MNRAS letter accepted

title: Probing horizonless compact objects through observable signatures and images of accretion disk
authors: Gargi Sen, Rajibul Shaikh, Sayan Chakrabarti, Santabrata Das
abstract: The observed images of M87$^*$ and Sgr A$^*$ by Event Horizon Telescope motivate us to study the spacetime geometry and accretion flow dynamics around compact objects beyond the Kerr/Schwarzschild scenario. In this work, we investigate the properties of a steady, inviscid, axisymmetric, advective accretion flow around the Zipoy-Voorhees ($\gamma$-metric) spacetime by solving the relativistic hydrodynamic equations. The $\gamma$-metric is a static, axisymmetric generalization of the Schwarzschild geometry and is characterized by a mass ($M_\bullet$) and a deformation parameter ($\gamma$). We examine how the deformation parameter $\gamma$ influences the effective potential, the location and nature of the critical points, and the resulting accretion flow topologies. Then, using relativistic thermal bremsstrahlung emissivity, we compute the spectral energy distribution and bolometric luminosity of the flow. We find that $\gamma$ affects the luminosity in opposite ways for the flow having outer critical point (O-type) and that having inner critical point (I-type). Finally, combining the flow properties with general relativistic ray tracing, we construct synthetic images of the accretion disk for different values of $\gamma$ and observer inclination angles. The resulting observed flux distribution independently confirms the trends obtained from the luminosity and spectral analyses. Although the shadow of the $\gamma$-metric has been shown to be consistent with the observed shadow radii of M87$^*$ and Sgr A$^*$, its accretion flow topology, the resulting radiative properties and image differ from the Schwarzschild case, thereby giving a complementary way to probe the deviations from the Schwarzschild paradigm.

title: Maximising the Open Magnetic Flux of a Star
authors: Anthony R. Yeates
abstract: We consider how to distribute the magnetic flux on a star's surface in order to maximise the proportion of open magnetic flux predicted by the potential field source surface model. The proportion of open flux is shown to be maximised by concentrating all of the positive and negative flux at antipodal points. For a typical source surface height, this enhances the open flux by 35% compared to a dipolar distribution. Even if the flux is spread over finite polar caps -- as on the Sun around Solar Minimum -- the open flux is still substantially enhanced compared to the dipole. Nevertheless, we show that the dipole approximation over-estimates the open flux for this kind of flux distribution.

title: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion
authors: Viraj Karambelkar, Kishalay De, Karel D. Temmink, Brian D. Metzger, Nadejda Blagorodnova, G. C. Anupama, Sudhanshu Barway, Judhajeet Basu, Eric C. Bellm, Varun Bhalerao, Aleksandra Bochenek, Shatakshi Chamoli, Kaustav Das, Christoffer Fremling, Danielle Frostig, Marco A. Gomez-Munoz, Steven L. Groom, K-Ryan Hinds, Joahan Castaneda Jaimes, Jacob Jencson, David Jones, Mansi Kasliwal, Grace Katusiime, Rubina Kotak, S. R. Kulkarni, Ryan Lau, Chang Liu, Nathan P. Lourie, Morgan MacLeod, Keiichi Maeda, Zoe McGrath, Geoffrey Mo, Gerard Garcia-Moreno, Josiah Purdum, Nabeel Rehemtulla, R. Michael Rich, Reed L. Riddle, Sam Rose, Robert A. Simcoe, Jesper Sollerman, Robert Stein, Hugo Tranin, Maxime Wavasseur, Simon de Wet, Jacob Wise
abstract: The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars. This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution (CEE), when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here, we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, that originates from the CEE of a ~7M$_{\odot}$ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as a ~0.7M$_{\odot}$ companion inspiraling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven year period of gradual brightening - the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core within a few (<10) orbits powers the ejection of the outermost ~10% of the stellar envelope at speeds ~10x the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope, $0.01\lesssim \alpha \lesssim 0.4$. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys.

title: Excess intergalactic heating around a dual quasar system 2.8 Gyr after the Big Bang
authors: Kirsten R. Hall, Nadia L. Zakamska, Jake S. Bennett, Yu-Ching Chen, Xiaohui Fan
abstract: Galaxy formation models necessitate that actively growing supermassive black holes, or quasars, strongly impact their environments. Theory suggests that quasar winds produce very hot gas bubbles that extend through the host galaxy and into the circumgalactic medium. Because this gas component is so hot and diffuse, the only way to measure its total energy is through the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect. Here we report the discovery of a dual quasar system at z=2.37 which is embedded in a bubble of hot gas as detected (at 6 $\sigma$) by a tSZ flux decrement at millimeter wavelengths. The total thermal energy of the hot gas is 9.7 x 10$^{60}$ erg. This energy exceeds the amount expected from all of the hot gas in a 10$^{13}$ M$_\odot$ dark matter halo by a factor of 3.6, and constitutes at least 0.6% of the quasar's lifetime energy output. We also find evidence for hot gas on larger (100-600 kpc) scales that may also originate in quasar outflows. This considerable excess energy is more than sufficient to shut off star formation and heat the intergalactic medium, implying a significant impact from quasar-driven winds on their surroundings. Such feedback plausibly explains the steep decline of the bright end of the luminosity function of galaxies across the observable Universe, and thus provides evidence to further support leading galaxy evolution theory.

title: JEPA for astronomy: multi-survey spectral alignment puts stellar parameters on the leading principal axes
authors: Xiaosheng Zhao, Rosemary F.G. Wyse, Yuan-Sen Ting, Alexander S. Szalay
abstract: Spectra from different surveys carry different systematics and are not calibrated against one another. Multi-survey foundation models for stellar spectra are then built by aligning embeddings of the same star observed across surveys. Most in astronomy follow the recipes established for language and vision, aligning with a contrastive loss that separates every star from the others. However, this does not ensure that the stellar physics is encoded in a form that a simple read-out can recover. Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed and varying only the alignment loss, we measure what an objective encodes from the principal-component geometry of the Gaia BP/RP (XP) spectra and from a linear probe of the stellar parameters. In a properly aligned embedding, the leading two principal components form a plane that recovers an analog of the Kiel diagram, the third component tracks [Fe/H], and [alpha/Fe] varies coherently across the plane, such that the chemically defined Galactic disks and accreted populations occupy distinct loci. We show that legibility, the ease of reading the information out, is highest for a training objective that never pushes stars apart, and instead constrains only the overall distribution of each survey's embeddings (JEPA). JEPA also exceeds the contrastive alternative at the same architecture, and the performance improves further as more surveys (Gaia XP+LAMOST LRS+DESI+APOGEE) are included. Predicted abundances for 8.0 million XP giants reproduce the main [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] structure of the Milky Way. These results indicate that the choice of alignment objective, not alignment alone, determines whether stellar labels are linearly recoverable.
comments: 15 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to AAS journals. Comments welcome

figs.cap: Multi-survey alignment. Embeddings from reconstructive autoencoders are mapped by a survey-specific head into a shared embedding space. Alignment is performed in a subsequent projection space (not shown for simplicity), which is discarded after training. Since the views share the same star, the common information is dominated by the underlying physical state (center), while instrument-specific information is suppressed. PCA and linear probes are then applied to aligned embeddings from a specific survey (e.g., Gaia).

Linear legibility of [Fe/H]. Each panel shows the first two principal components, PC1 and PC2, colored by PC3, from embeddings of two alignment models (JEPA, top left; CLIP, bottom left) and one unaligned autoencoder (AE, bottom right). The APOGEE Kiel diagram colored by [Fe/H] (top right) is shown as the physical anchor. Components are computed independently for each panel and are in arbitrary units. The same $40{,}000$ stars are shown throughout. Reconstruction alone (AE) leaves [Fe/H] unordered. In contrast, alignment recovers the ordering, and the objective determines how sharply it is recovered (JEPA vs CLIP).

Gravity and chemistry encoding. The same PC1–PC2 plane as in Figure 2 is shown for the JEPA model, colored by surface gravity $\log g$ (left), by [$\alpha$/Fe] (middle), and by chemical category (right, where gray marks unclassified stars and thin/thick/accreted/VMP/low-$\alpha$ & MP contain $46{,}627/19{,}340/9{,}292/143/5{,}470$ stars). The plane is ordered by surface gravity. The chemical populations occupy distinct bands whose [$\alpha$/Fe] matches their chemical definition.

The [$\alpha$/Fe]–[Fe/H] plane of $8.0$ million Gaia XP red giant stars ($T_{\rm eff}<5300$ K, $\log g<3.5$) with median per-pixel S/N $\geq 64$ and full phase-space information, in bins of Galactocentric radius $R$ in the midplane and height $|z|$. The elemental abundances are predicted from the aligned XP embedding of the JEPA model. The main chemical structures of the MW are recovered from resolving power $\sim 50$ XP spectra alone.

Architecture of four-survey JEPA. Each survey spectrum is encoded by a frozen reconstructive backbone (an overcomplete autoencoder for Gaia XP, masked transformers for LAMOST LRS and DESI, and a wavelength-aware autoencoder built on the universal spectral tokenizer for APOGEE; labeled AE, MT and UST, respectively) and is then mapped onto a common 768-dimensional representation by a trainable head: an MLP for the single XP latent vector, and cross-attention pooling for the token sequences of the other three surveys. A single rectified projector, shared by all four surveys, maps these representations into a 128-dimensional non-negative space. A mean-squared invariance term aligns the representations across the six cross-matched survey edges, pulling different views of the same star towards a common point. A per-survey rectified distribution-matching regularization (RDMReg) prevents collapse constraint without requiring negative pairs. Only the heads and the shared projector are trained (33.8 M parameters, against 142 M held frozen). All downstream probes read the head output before the projector (dashed arrow), so the recovered stellar parameters come from the 768-dimensional head representation rather than from the loss-space projection.

title: Fuzzy Dark Matter as a diffractive barrier: Wave-optics Signatures of Ultralight Fields on Lensed Gravitational Waves
authors: Manish Tamta, Han Gil Choi, Diego Blas, Miguel Zumalacárregui
abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) propagate through the universe from sources at high redshift, experiencing the gravitational fields of the intervening matter distribution. Halos composed of ultralight dark matter (ULDM) contain strong density fluctuations, reflecting the interference pattern in the field distribution of the ultralight bosons. In the wave-optics regime, ULDM fluctuations act as a diffractive grating, imprinting frequency-dependent modulations of GWs, in addition to magnification and other gravitational lensing effects. Since lensing depends on the projected surface density, we derive its approximate probability distribution and show how it departs from a Gaussian distribution depending on the halo profile and coherence length. We then quantify how the GW diffraction signatures produced by the granules depend on macroimage magnification and parity. The ULDM interference network imprints stochastic diffraction fluctuations at the $O(1)\%$ level on GWs moderately lensed by the host when the Fresnel scale is comparable to the granule coherence length $r_F(f)\sim\ell_c$. These fluctuations can be enhanced to $\gtrsim10\%$ when the host macroimage forms near the critical curve or for Type II macroimages. For massive black hole binaries observed by LISA, the diffraction signature can be detectable around the ULDM particle mass $m_\phi\sim10^{-21}$ eV, providing either a smoking-gun signature of ULDM or new constraints on $m_\phi$.
comments: 24 pages revtex4 + references, 10 figures, 1 table

title: The Science and Technology of Broad-Band X-ray Astrophysics
authors: Broad-Band X-ray Science Analysis Group, Chien-Ting Chen, Kristin K. Madsen, Daniel Stern, Javier A. García, Xiurui Zhao, Alaa Salah Afifi, Adrianah Appleman, Steve Bongiorno, Matteo Bachetti, Peter Boorman, Mckinley Brumback, Douglas Buisson, Filippo D'Ammando, Kirtan Dixit, Rahul Gupta, Danielle Gurgew, Gaurava K. Jaisawal, Phil Kaaret, Renee Ludlam, Peter Maksym, Labani Mallick, Eric Miller, Kaya Mori, Emanuele Nardini, Srikanth Panini Singam, Mark Reynolds, M. Lynnie Saade, Aarran Shaw, Dustin Swarm, Nicholas Thomas, Georgios Vasilopoulos, Dom Walton, Gaurav Waratkar, Dan Wilkins, Jooyun Woo, Yi-Jung Yang
abstract: Much of our understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena over the past decade has relied on coordinated observations extending from soft X-rays (<10 keV) to hard X-rays (>10 keV). While soft X-ray facilities remain abundant, focusing capabilities above ~10 keV are scarce, representing the primary gap for broad-band X-ray science. Simultaneous wide-band observations are essential to study thermal and non-thermal processes in extreme environments such as accretion discs, jets, and coronae. However, current high-energy observations remain limited by a lack of high angular resolution and sensitivity beyond Chandra's bandpass. With upcoming multi-messenger facilities set to dramatically increase variable and transient sources, a high angular resolution broad-band X-ray mission is critically needed. This report reviews the current landscape of high-energy facilities, outlines key science drivers, focusing on extragalactic accretion (the cosmic X-ray background) and Galactic compact objects, and examines the underlying technology landscape, including optics and detectors. Broad-band X-ray astrophysics is primed to address key questions from the Astro2020 Decadal Survey. While past focusing efforts have been limited to the Small Explorer class, technological advances now enable low-risk Probe- or Flagship-class architectures capable of delivering order-of-magnitude improvements in capabilities.
comments: BBX-SAG Co-Chairs: Chien-Ting Chen (MSFC), Kristin K. Madsen (GSFC) & Daniel Stern (JPL). A report to the NASA Astrophysics Leadership and the Physics of the Cosmos Program office by the Broad-band X-ray Science Analysis Group this https URL

title: A higher-order smoothness indicator as refinement criterion for Newtonian and relativistic MHD simulations
authors: Samuel Solod, Yoonsoo Kim, Elias R. Most
abstract: Adaptive mesh refinement is a widely adopted strategy for grid-based numerical simulation codes to mitigate the high computational cost of multi-length scale problems. A robust and reliable mesh refinement criterion with minimal requirement for problem-specific tuning is critical for efficient and accurate simulations. Motivated by the oscillation indicators used in the spectral methods literature, we develop a new mesh refinement criterion employing a 5-point stencil for multi-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations, essentially extending the conventional 3-point Löhner scheme. We implement the criterion in the astrophysical fluid dynamics code AthenaK and test it across a variety of benchmark problems in Newtonian, special relativistic, and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, demonstrating its robustness and versatility.
comments: 18 pages, 15 figures

abstract: Redrock is a software package for spectroscopic classification and redshift fitting, designed to use the full information from spectroperfectionism outputs: flux-calibrated spectra, uncorrelated errors, and a per-spectrum resolution matrix encoding the non-Gaussian wavelength-dependent spectral line-spread function. Redrock was originally developed for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), but the Extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS) also used Redrock as their primary galaxy redshift fitter prior to DESI. This paper presents the algorithmic details of Redrock and its performance on DESI data. On spectra from DESI DR2, Redrock achieves a redshift recovery rate of approximately 98% for the Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) and Luminous Red Galaxies (LRG), 95.9% for Emission Line Galaxies (ELG), and 92.6% for quasars (QSO), and it delivers unbiased stellar radial velocities with a precision of roughly 5 km/s.
comments: Submitted to AJ

title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
authors: Ralf Greve, Björn Grieger, Oliver J. Stenzel
abstract: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.
comments: 12 pages, 6 figures

figs.cap: Modular structure of MAIC-2 v2.3. All initializations are done in the main program maic2. This includes reading the physical parameters and the set-up from the run-specs header file maic2_specs_<run_name>.h, where <run_name> is a placeholder for the name of the simulation to be carried out. In the main loop (numerical forward-in-time integration), maic2 carries out three steps: (1) Use the module boundary_maic2_m to update the orbital parameters, compute the surface temperature (LIT scheme, module instemp_m) and the surface mass balance for H$_{2}$O ice (evaporation, atmospheric water transport and condensation, module evap_cond_m); (2) use the module calc_top_maic2_m to update the topography (thickness) of the H$_{2}$O ice deposits; (3) use the module output_m for data output in ASCII format. Auxiliary modules are maic2_types_m for declarations of kind types, maic2_variables_m for declarations of global variables, and maic2_maths_m for required mathematical tools.

title: Stars and gas in the most metal-poor galaxies -- II. Search for VMS and determination of stellar population and nebular properties at $Z\lesssim0.1\,Z_\odot$
authors: Aida Wofford, Oskar Aranguré, Christophe Morisset, Calum Hawcroft, Claus Leitherer, Svea Hernández, Gustavo Bruzual, Stephane Charlot
abstract: Constraining the properties of OB-star populations and ionized gas at low metallicity is essential for understanding a broad range of astrophysical objects, from stellar black holes to the first galaxies. Rest-frame UV spectra of nearby metal-poor galaxies provide crucial constraints on theoretical predictions of low-metallicity stars and gas. However, such spectra are scarce at $Z\lesssim0.1Z\,\odot$, and candidate Very Massive Stars (VMS) remain elusive. We analyse optical and new UV spectra of nearby star-forming galaxies with $Z\lesssim0.1Z\,\odot$, selected for their nebular He II $\lambda4686$ emission and lack of Wolf-Rayet blue and red bumps, making them promising targets for VMS searches. Some galaxies exhibit stellar wind features (group 1), while others do not (group 2). For group 1, we compare STARBURST99, GALAXEV, and BPASS predictions with observed stellar lines to constrain OB-population ages and masses. The inferred ages are too old for VMS to be present. We also use pySTARBURST99 and GALAXEV photoionization models to investigate the ionized gas in a subsample, finding no evidence for VMS-dominated ionization. The absence of detected VMS may reflect their rarity, our limited sample size, or shortcomings in current models. Moreover, reproducing the extreme optical and UV line ratios simultaneously requires unrealistic N/O, ionization parameters, or Lyman continuum escape fractions, suggesting that multiple ionizing-source populations may be needed.
comments: Accepted for publication

title: Strongly Suppressed Cosmic-Ray Diffusion in a Wind-Blown Cavity Environment of SNR G21.8-3.0
authors: Yuan Li, Gwenael Giacinti, Yang Su, Xiao Zhang, Hui Li, Yang Chen
abstract: We report the discovery of a GeV $\gamma$-ray source spatially offset from SNR G21.8-3.0, while no significant high-energy emission is detected from the remnant itself. Using 16 yr of \emph{Fermi}-LAT observations together with $^{12}$CO ($J=1-0$) data, we show that the GeV emission is spatially associated with a localized molecular cloud located just outside a gas cavity whose boundary closely follows the SNR shell. This configuration supports a scenario in which cosmic rays (CRs) escaping from the remnant propagate through a progenitor-carved low-density cavity and illuminate nearby dense gas. Modeling of the cloud emission requires a diffusion coefficient suppressed by a factor of several tens relative to the canonical Galactic value, indicating strongly inhibited CR transport around the remnant. Rather than serving as a simple low-density escape channel, the wind-blown cavity appears to regulate CR propagation through local magnetic structure and enhanced turbulence. This system therefore provides evidence that circumstellar structures can control the escape and early transport of CRs around supernova remnants.
comments: 10 pages, 5 figures, submitted

title: Subsequent Dust-Fading Events of the Wolf-Rayet Star WR 59: A Continuous Visual Record
authors: Rod Stubbings
abstract: This paper presents long-term visual and space-based monitoring of the WC9d Wolf-Rayet star WR 59 from 2017 to 2026, documenting a profound physical transition from a stable baseline to an ongoing phase of continuous dust production. Visual observations using a 22-inch telescope initially established a four-year quiescent baseline at magnitude 13.9. Following the historic May 2021 discovery fade to magnitude 15.2, long-term nightly visual monitoring documented an accelerating sequence of twelve distinct fading episodes over subsequent years, characterised by progressively shorter inter-fade recovery intervals. Due to severe pixel crowding and flux contamination from a close 11.7 V companion star 11 arcseconds away, automated large-pixel survey pipelines remain completely blind to these high-amplitude fading events. Direct comparisons with NASA's TESS satellite photometry during quiet phases show that targeted visual magnitude estimates measure systemic baseline micro-variations with professional accuracy while bridging space mission coverage gaps. High-density observation blocks during the minimum floor reveal a highly dynamic, rapid, minute-by-minute bimodal oscillation and sub-minute flickering between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2. At the time of writing, the system remains locked in an unprecedented deep minimum, varying between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2 for a sustained period exceeding 102 consecutive days. Intensive visual monitoring is ongoing to record the eventual egress recovery profile.
comments: 43 pages, 26 figures, 21 tables. Presents 9 years of unblended visual monitoring of WR 59 (2017-2026), including master chronological logs, high-density intra-night runs, light curves, and TESS space-based overlays. Summary report to appear in the British Astronomical Association Variable Star Section (BAA VSS) Circular No. 211, March 1, 2027

title: The Population of Radio Hypernebulae from Mass-Transferring Massive Binaries
authors: Kohki Uno, Brian D. Metzger, Navin Sridhar, Lieke A. C. van Son, Floor S. Broekgaarden, Dillon Z. Dong, Keiichi Maeda
abstract: Massive binary evolution is punctuated by brief phases of highly super-Eddington mass transfer (MT) onto neutron stars and black holes, presaging luminous transients such as supernovae, common envelope events, and gravitational wave sources. These hyper-accreting phases power relativistic jets and slower mass-loaded outflows, inflating extended nebulae of relativistic particles. Though observed in the local universe as ultra-luminous X-ray binaries and micro-quasars, the present census is biased against shorter-lived and hence rarer but potentially even more extreme MT systems: so-called ``hypernebulae'' (HNbe). We use the binary population synthesis code (\textsc{COMPAS}) to estimate the MT population, which spans a wide range of MT rates $\dot{M} \sim 10^{2-7}\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$ and source lifetimes $t_{\rm acc} \sim 10^{0-6}$ years. Combining this synthetic population with a semi-analytic model for their time-dependent radio emission, we predict the observable properties of HNbe over cosmic time. HNbe exhibit a broad GHz luminosity range extending to $L_{\nu, \rm peak} \sim 10^{28-30}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$, and up to $\sim 10^{2}$ ($\sim 10^{5}$) HNbe are detectable by the wide-field radio surveys VLASS (DSA-2000) in our conservative model. A fraction of these systems should possess angular sizes and spatial offsets from star-forming regions (due to the first supernova kick) resolvable by VLBI. The most luminous donors, helium Hertzsprung-gap stars, may be detectable coincident with radio HNbe with Roman imaging out to distances $\sim 30$\,Mpc. Our findings suggest HNbe as promising probes of the pathways linking massive binaries to energetic transients.
comments: 27 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables. submitted

title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b
authors: Tasneem Basra Khan, Liton Majumdar, Mithun Patra, Tonmoy Deka, Swastik Dewan, Priyankush Ghosh, Vishal Meena
abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.
comments: 28 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables. Revised and resubmitted to The Astronomical Journal. We thank the anonymous referee for their constructive comments. Further comments are welcome

title: Zippers and Twisters II: The lopsidedness of satellite systems around local massive galaxies emerges from a shifting cosmic web landscape
authors: Janvi P. Madhani, Charlotte Welker, Sneha Nair, Katarina Kraljic, Christophe Pichon, Yohan Dubois
abstract: We investigate the role of the cosmic web on the origin and strength of lopsidedness in the distributions of luminous dwarf satellites around massive galaxies analogs in the high-resolution hydrodynamic simulation NewHorizon. Using common lopsidedness estimators, we find that $>25\%$ of our sample display ``statistically significant" lopsidedness incompatible with expectations for dark matter sub-haloes. The NewHorizon sample is generally skewed towards being more lopsided than naive expectations. This cautions against using dark matter or under-resolved hydrodynamic simulations as a null-hypothesis to compare to real systems. We find broad, hemispheric lopsidedness to be much more prevalent than narrow lopsidedness inherited from group infall. Across all systems, the dividing plane between the richest and emptiest hemispheres is systematically aligned with a nearby intermediate-scale cosmic filament. Further analysis reveals that the lopsidedness of systems is largely inherited from that of the network of filaments feeding them. The most populated side almost systematically contains the highest number of filaments. Such anisotropies of local filament networks are often indicative of on-going or recent zippers (filament merger $<2$ Gyr). Converging filamentary structures therefore funnel satellites preferentially onto one side of host halos, naturally generating lopsided configurations without requiring galaxy mergers. Twister remnants (of high orbital momentum mergers of filaments) are also found on the richest hemisphere of our systems, perhaps reminiscent of vorticity preventing mergers hence causing satellites' pooling. These results suggest that lopsidedness is primarily an outcome of the evolution of the intermediate-scale cosmic web. This highlights the need for increased hydrodynamic resolution in simulations.
comments: 26 pages, 20 figures, Submitted to ApJ

title: Inverse Reconstruction of Two-Field Potentials for a DESI-Motivated Phantom-Divide Transition
authors: Tonghua Liu, Xiaolei Li, Marek Biesiada, Tian-Nuo Li, Jun-Qian Jiang, Arman Shafieloo, Xin Zhang
abstract: A phantom-divide transition favored by recent cosmological observations poses an inverse problem: which field potentials realize the inferred expansion history, and what features are uniquely fixed by it? We reconstruct local potentials for a canonical-phantom scalar pair with standard matter and radiation, targeting Metastable Emergent Dark Energy histories constrained by CMB, DESI BAO, and Type Ia supernova data. The coupled-field Friedmann evolution reproduces the target background to numerical accuracy across the transition, with regular perturbations through the crossing. At the phantom divide, the transition slope sets a dimensionless potential-energy release rate insensitive to the partition of kinetic energy. We identify local potential deformations that preserve both background expansion and linear dynamics. This construction gives a classical field realization of the inferred transition and disentangles observationally fixed energy balances from interaction terms requiring additional theoretical input.
comments: 17 pages, 8 figures, comments are welcome

title: The Geometric Imprint of a Tilted Accretion Disk in Gravitational Waves
authors: Jing-Ze Xia, Chen Yuan
abstract: Gravitational wave astronomy has opened a new window onto black holes and the dynamics of strong-field gravity, while accretion flows offer a complementary and natural laboratory for probing strong-field physics. In this work, we show that the gravitational wave emission from an initially tilted accretion disk carries a distinct imprint of its orientation. We perform three dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations and evaluate the gravitational waves through Teukolsky equation. For an aligned disk, the emission is concentrated in low-$|m|$ modes, where $m$ is the azimuthal quantum number. For the initially tilted disk, higher-$|m|$ modes make a larger relative contribution. As the tilted flow subsequently aligns with the black hole spin, the contribution of $|m|\ge2$ modes decreases, showing strong correlation with the tilt angle. This indicates that the gravitational waves generated by the black hole environment carries geometric information about the surrounding matter. Our results establish a route towards using multimode gravitational radiation to probe the geometry and dynamical evolution of accretion flows in the strong-field region.
comments: 8 pages, 4 figures

title: Constraining Accretion Heating in Neutron Stars with Carbon Instability and Quiescent Cooling
authors: Chengze Hou, Amira Aoyama, Akira Dohi
abstract: In accreting neutron stars, different heating depths can produce similar quiescent cooling when the heating strength and core temperature are adjusted. For KS 1731-260, we compare thermal histories with accretion heating either in a shallower region that overlaps the carbon fuel layer or in a deeper region below it. Without the carbon instability condition, the two histories fit ten quiescent Chandra spectra nearly equally well. When local carbon instability is required at the observed superburst epoch, the deeper region needs stronger accretion heating than the shallower region. After the thermal and spectral parameters are refitted, the deeper history retains more heat beneath the fuel and produces excess early quiescent emission. A larger fitted absorbing column partly attenuates this excess but makes the late spectra too faint. The fuel temperatures at the superburst epoch are similar in the two histories, so the same prescribed energy release produces nearly identical superburst decays. Including carbon burial, consumption and nuclear heating reduces the accretion heating needed for rapid burning to begin near the observed superburst; shallower heating still fits the quiescent spectra better. This preference persists across the tested fuel depths, fusion rates, distances and absorption treatments. In synthetic examples, carbon in older material allows deeper heating to match the cooling of a shallower-heating reference. Inferring the heating location therefore requires a fuel distribution and thermal history consistent with ignition, burst emission and quiescent cooling.
comments: 21 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal

title: Positron escape from dark matter spikes in black hole X-ray binaries
authors: Mpho Kgoadi, Geoff Beck
abstract: Chan and Lee present a model where the AMS-02 positron excess is explained by dark matter (DM) annihilation in spike halos around nearby black holes A0620-00 and XTE J1118+480. Their model assumes a uniform magnetic and diffusive environment en route to Earth. Thus, it depends on the assumption that one can ignore the small-scale, near-horizon environment in the diffusion-loss equation. We demonstrate that this is not the case. An accurate magnetic field model near the horizon means, without increasing the required cross-section by a factor of roughly 500 to 1400, depending on the transport near the horizon, the positron flux from these sources cannot account for a significant fraction of the AMS-02 excess.
comments: 9 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables

title: Two Faint Tidal Disruption Events Discovered in a Pilot Search with the Wide Field Survey Telescope
authors: Mingxin Wu, Ning Jiang, Jiazheng Zhu, Jianwei Lyu, Zheyu Lin, Yibo Wang, Tinggui Wang, Chengyi Wang, Weiyu Wu, Jie Lin, Zelin Xu, Minxuan Cai, Ranfang Zheng, Lulu fan, Ji-an Jiang, Xu Kong, Feng Li, Ming Liang, Binyang Liu, Zhen Wan, Hairen Wang, Jian Wang, Yongquan Xue, Hongfei Zhang, Wen Zhao, Xianzhong Zheng, Qingfeng Zhu
abstract: We report the discovery of TDE 2025alrm/WFST250129blnve and TDE 2025amkg/WFST251021dbmwk in the first six months of the wide-field survey (WFS) performed by the 2.5-meter Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST). Both events are apparently faint among known optical tidal disruption events (TDEs), with peak magnitudes of $g \sim 20.0$ and $g \sim 19.6$, respectively. Blackbody fits to the multi-band photometry yield roughly constant temperatures of $\sim 10^{4}$ K for both sources, with peak bolometric luminosities of $10^{43.6}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and $10^{43.8}$ erg s$^{-1}$, respectively. Optical spectra obtained during the declining phase display characteristic broad Balmer, He II, and N III emission lines, classifying both sources as H+He TDEs. Host-galaxy SED fitting suggests stellar masses on the order of $10^{9} M_{\odot}$ and black hole masses of $\sim10^{6} M_{\odot}$, which are typical of optically selected TDE hosts. The pilot discovery of these two faint TDEs along with dozens of candidates, demonstrates the capability of WFST to discover TDEs, owing to its exceptional survey depth. Furthermore, these events highlight the value of the $u$ band in multi-band surveys for TDE selection, particularly for distinguishing TDEs from supernovae at early phases. With continued operations, WFST is expected to substantially expand the known TDE population, especially by uncovering nearby low-luminosity events and high-redshift TDEs, both of which remain poorly explored.
comments: Accepted for publication in ApJ

title: Multifrequency deep radio continuum VLA observations toward OMC-2/3
authors: Ana K. Diaz-Rodriguez, Mayra Osorio, Guillem Anglada, S. Thomas Megeath, John J. Tobin, Elise Furlan, M. Dolores Hurtado-Espejo, A. Florin Placinta-Mitrea, José F. Gómez, Guillermo Blázquez-Calero, William J. Fischer, P. Manoj, Dan M. Watson, Amelia M. Stutz, Luis F. Rodríguez
abstract: We present multiwavelength (0.7-5 cm) Very Large Array continuum observations of high sensitivity (3 $\mu$Jy beam$^{-1}$), reaching an angular resolution of $0.4''$ (154 au) toward the Integral Shaped Filament in Orion. We image a field of $12.5'$ in diameter, containing the whole OMC-2 region and the southernmost $2.5'$ of OMC-3. We report the positions, flux densities and spectral indices of 47 radio sources, and discuss their nature. We conclude that, out of the 57 radio sources in the field of view, 36 (63%) are very likely tracing YSOs, 4 are tracing jet/outflow knots, and 6 are extragalactic sources; the nature of the remaining sources is unclear. We identify the driving sources of the 9 previously reported molecular outflows in our field of view. Four of them show a clear elongated radio jet morphology. We detect free-free emission from two potential photoevaporating discs associated with Class III YSOs. We find variability in 11 radio sources, 7 of which are also variable at shorter wavelengths. We find 7 pairs of radio sources with projected separations of 150-3000 au, which are potential binary systems; we identify a total of 17 potential multiple systems within this separation range when taking into account sources detected at other wavelengths. This work highlights the potential of deep VLA observations to uncover a large population of weak radio sources and study their diversity, serving as a guide for future surveys with the SKA and ngVLA.

title: Multi-epoch imaging observations of the Galactic Center with NIRCam and MIRI

abstract: The center of the Milky Way is the densest and most extreme environment in our Galaxy, its most active star forming region, and the only galaxy nucleus where we can resolve stars down to about a solar mass on the main sequence. The Galactic Center (GC) contains a nuclear stellar disk, a nuclear star cluster, and a supermassive black hole, all embedded within the so-called Central Molecular Zone, which showcases conditions of the interstellar medium that are typically found in high-redshift star-forming regions. The GC hosts the highest concentration of massive stars in the Milky Way and hosts a large concentration of rare objects, such as Wolf Rayet stars and X-ray binaries. The GC is therefore an astrophysical target of outstanding importance. A multi-epoch JWST program enables novel science including the lifetime of planet-forming disks, the search for intermediate mass black holes, direct measurements of the multi-scale gravitational potential, and a deep measurement of the star formation history. Multi-epoch imaging observations with JWST's NIRCam and MIRI instruments will go far beyond Roman WFI surveys in terms of depth and astrometric and photometric precision because of its $3\times$ better resolution, and it expands spectral coverage in narrow bands and mid-infrared wavelength coverage. The proposed observations would correspond to a Treasury Program of about 420\,h, distributed over three epochs spaced three to five years apart.

title: SPONGE: Sulphur, Phosphorus, Oxygen, Nitrogen, and carbon Galactic Evolution. I. CNOPS elements as probes of physical processes in stars and galaxies
authors: D. Romano, M. Limongi, E. Caffau, Y. P. Zou, P. Bonifacio, L. Monaco, L. Colzi, E. Spitoni, M. Palla, S. Tsiatsiou, D. Nandal, J. Alazzawi, A. Falla, F. Fontani, A. J. Gallagher, R. Hirschi, F. Lucertini, A. Mucciarelli, L. Roberti, M. Spite, M. Steffen
abstract: As fundamental bio-essential elements, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulphur (CNOPS) warrant a precise mapping of their cosmic origins. In this paper, we present the SPONGE project (Sulphur, Phosphorus, Oxygen, Nitrogen, and carbon Galactic Evolution), aimed at establishing a self-consistent galactic chemical evolution (GCE) framework capable of simultaneously reproducing local abundance benchmarks along with key observational constraints in external galaxies. Here, we focus on the Milky Way. We compile literature data and construct GCE models incorporating various single- and binary-star yields, taking stellar rotation and nova nucleosynthesis into account. Fast rotators are confirmed to be essential for primary 14N and 13C production at low metallicities. Although our homogeneous models do not reach the lowest 12C/13C ratios observed in some halo stars, this discrepancy should not be taken as a refutation of the model, as observational selection effects may apply. Predicted C and N isotopic ratios along the disc agree remarkably well with those inferred from radio observations of star-forming regions. Notably, our models explain Galactic P enrichment as originating predominantly from massive stars, without any ad hoc adjustment of the yields or the need for a significant nova contribution. Conversely, novae are required to synthesize non-negligible fractions of 13C and 15N. Optimizing GCE trajectories against a comprehensive CNOPS ensemble simultaneously, rather than single diagnostics one at a time, establishes a robust baseline for future work. Remaining open questions, such as the predicted overproduction of 12C at low metallicities and 34S along the disc, alongside the abundance scatter of some key elements, provide concrete targets for subsequent papers in this series.

title: Probing the Turbulent Magnetised Interstellar Medium of the Small Magellanic Cloud through Depolarisation with POSSUM Observations
authors: Jason M. Price, Yik Ki Ma, Amit Seta, N. M. McClure-Griffiths, B. M. Gaensler, S. Lyla Jung, Cameron L. Van Eck, David McConnell, Lindsey Oberhelman, J. D. Livingston, Takuya Akahori, Shane P. O'Sullivan, Denis Leahy, C. S. Anderson
abstract: The interstellar medium (ISM) of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) provides a unique laboratory for studying magnetised gas in a low-metallicity, tidally disturbed environment. We investigate this magnetised turbulent medium using broad-band polarimetric data from the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP)'s Polarisation Sky Survey of the Universe's Magnetism (POSSUM), leveraging a high-density Rotation Measure (RM) grid comprising 951 RMs ($\sim24$ RMs per square degree) to probe the magneto-ionic structure of the SMC. We statistically compare the number densities of polarised and non-polarised non-thermal background sources on a per-square-degree basis, revealing spatially coherent depolarisation signatures that correlate with enhanced plane-of-sky RM fluctuations. This is consistent with a turbulent cascade from large-scale structures. Analysed through RM synthesis and Stokes $QU$-fitting, we attribute the depolarisation to a turbulent magneto-ionic medium within the telescope's beam ($\lesssim6~\mathrm{pc}$). Faraday complexity is detected in $\sim$24% of the RM sources; however, no coherent spatial structure is observed in the complexity distribution, and we attribute this primarily to internal source structure or an extended halo surrounding the SMC rather than to its main body. Furthermore, as previously identified in the Large Magellanic Cloud, depolarisation in the SMC increases with emission measure; however, the underlying Faraday dispersion is $\sim$6 times weaker. With the thermal electron density smooth on the scales of the field fluctuations, this depolarisation is likely driven by magnetic field fluctuations.

title: A Butterfly Collector's View of Fast Radio Bursts: Repeating Sources Go Quiet within a Few Years
authors: Shotaro Yamasaki
abstract: How long repeating fast radio burst (FRB) sources stay active is key to their origins but poorly known as a population. We test this with unseen species estimation, a method first used to predict how many new butterfly species a further collecting trip would find. If each source keeps the same mean rate over time, the number of sources seen $k+1$ times in one window predicts how many bursts the sources seen $k$ times will emit in a later window. It assumes neither the burst rate distribution nor source distances. For the five years of CHIME/FRB Catalog 2, we measure the ratio $R$ of observed to predicted bursts against the gap $\Delta$ between windows. A steady mean rate gives $R = 1$ at every $\Delta$, so a change of $R$ with $\Delta$ means that the sources change. $R$ is close to unity for $\Delta \lesssim 60$ days and drops by half within one year. Neither steady nor randomly fluctuating sources reproduce this decline, unless the latter are mostly silent. Three models explain the data equally well: a lifetime of about three years, on/off activity with two-year active phases, or a mix of short- and long-lived sources. Fitted to the first three years alone, they correctly predict the further decline of $R$ in the last two years. Longer monitoring of $R$, and of whether silent sources come back to life, will distinguish them. Unlike butterfly species, FRB sources do not wait for the next collecting trip, so follow-up should start soon.

title: WFST0533buha (Bi'an): A Fast Blue Ultraluminous Transient Candidate with Unusual Blue/NUV Colors
authors: Zelin Xu, Ji-an Jiang, Ziqing Jia, Keiichi Maeda, Dezheng Meng, Zhengyan Liu, Weiyu Wu, Junhan Zhao, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Lluís Galbany, Saurabh W. Connolly, Tao An, Ming Chen, Zigao Dai, Xu Kong, Tiancheng Lv, Masaomi Tanaka, Nozomu Tominaga, Ailing Wang, Ning Jiang, Yongquan Xue, Wen Zhao, Qingfeng Zhu, Lulu Fan, Feng Li, Ming Liang, Binyang Liu, Zhen Wan, Hairen Wang, Jian Wang, Ji Yang, Hongfei Zhang, Xianzhong Zheng
abstract: We present WFST0533buha (Bi'an), a fast blue ultraluminous transient (FBUT) candidate discovered by the Wide Field Survey Telescope Deep High-cadence $ugr$-band Survey. The source brightened by approximately 2.5 mag in $u$ within 3 days and has a half-maximum timescale ($t_{1/2}$) shorter than 6 days. Two spectra show a blue, featureless continuum but do not provide a secure redshift. Einstein Probe observations yield only X-ray upper limits, while a faint radio counterpart was detected at 15 GHz with the VLA. The early $u$-band detection and intensive multiband coverage of Bi'an demonstrate the value of deep, high-cadence blue-band observations for discovering and characterizing FBUTs at early phases. Notably, Bi'an shows redder blue/NUV colors than AT 2018cow and AT 2024wpp, suggesting possible diversity in the short-wavelength properties of FBUTs.
