title: SN 2025wiu: A Slowly Evolving Type Ib Supernova with an Extraordinary Post-maximum Bump
authors: Zhengyan Liu, Ji-an Jiang, Zelin Xu, Qiliang Fang, Keiichi Maeda, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Lluís Galbany, Saurabh W. Jha, Željko Ivezić, Peter Yoachim, Andrew J. Connolly, Dezheng Meng, Weiyu Wu, Ziqing Jia, Niko Pyykkinen, Masaomi Tanaka, Nozomu Tominaga, Junhan Zhao, Ming Chen, Tiancheng Lv, Tinggui Wang, Zigao Dai, Xu Kong, Luhan Li, Bo Wang, Jianguo Wang, Yongquan Xue, Wen Zhao, Qingfeng Zhu, Lulu Fan, Feng Li, Ming Liang, Binyang Liu, Zhen Wan, Hairen Wang, Jian Wang, Ji Yang, Hongfei Zhang, Xianzhong Zheng
abstract: Stripped-envelope supernovae (SESNe) originate from massive progenitors that have lost most or all of their outer envelopes prior to core collapse. Recent advances in optical time-domain surveys have revealed a growing population of peculiar SESNe with unusual light-curve morphologies, pointing to energy sources beyond the standard radioactive-decay scenario. In this work, we present multi-band photometric and spectroscopic observations of SN 2025wiu, a peculiar Type Ib supernova discovered by the Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST). SN 2025wiu is characterized by a high luminosity and exceptionally slow photometric evolution, with a prominent post-maximum bump peaking at $\sim50$ days after the primary maximum. Its early light curve also shows a weak excess consistent with shock-cooling emission from a compact progenitor with a radius of $\sim4\,R_\odot$. The spectra show only modest evolution, with persistently weak line features and no narrow emission lines detected even at $\sim110$ days after maximum. By modeling the primary peak and late-time tail with a combination of radioactive decay and additional energy sources, we isolate the post-maximum bump, which has a roughly symmetric profile with a peak luminosity of $\sim2.4 \times 10^{42}~\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ and a characteristic duration of $\sim42$ days. We discuss circumstellar medium (CSM) interaction, accretion, magnetar activity, and a double $^{56}$Ni distribution as possible origins of the bump. The latter three scenarios face challenges in reproducing the post-maximum bump, while delayed CSM interaction remains a possible explanation.

title: A Tight Broad-line Width-Luminosity Relation in Little Red Dots and Its Consequence for Virial Black Hole Masses
authors: Haoyu Wang
abstract: JWST has uncovered compact high-redshift sources with red, $\sim 5000$ K optical continua and broad Balmer lines, known as "little red dots" (LRDs). Whether these lines trace gas orbiting a massive black hole or electron scattering in a dense, Eddington-limited envelope around a lighter black hole leaves inferred masses spanning $10^{4}$--$10^{8}\,M_\odot$. We test both pictures by uniformly refitting public JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 29 LRDs, 15 other JWST broad-line sources, and luminosity-matched SDSS quasars. At fixed $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ luminosity, LRD broad $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ widths are remarkably uniform: their intrinsic scatter is 0.054 dex ($<0.075$ dex at 95%), less than half that of quasars (0.12 dex), clustering near $1760\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ outside the three brightest sources. Because single-epoch virial masses scale as width squared, they scatter intrinsically by $<0.16$ dex at fixed $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ luminosity, making virial masses and mass functions nearly deterministic restatements of luminosity regardless of the underlying physics. Compared with the Keplerian speed $v_{\rm K}$ at the photosphere of an Eddington-limited envelope, computed from each source's measured continuum luminosity and temperature, observed widths are $2.5$--$3.0\,v_{\rm K}$ ($2\text{--}3\times$ standard expectations for virial factors $f_{\rm vir}\approx0.5\text{--}1$), with a quarter of the flux above escape speed and no detected continuum-luminosity dependence at fixed $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ luminosity. Bound orbits outside a spherical photosphere thus require sub-Eddington luminosities ($\leq 0.10\text{--}0.30\,L_{\rm Edd}$), whereas an Eddington or super-Eddington envelope requires uniform $2\text{--}3\times$ non-gravitational broadening within the $\mathrm{H}\alpha$-emitting gas.

abstract: Cosmic-ray particles in the TeV range, originating outside the solar system, are partially blocked on their way to Earth by the Moon, producing a deficit in their flux known as the Moon shadow. This work presents a precision measurement of the westward shift of the Moon's shadow using 3.4 years of data from LHAASO's Water Cherenkov Detector Array (WCDA). We use this direct physical measurement, combined with four cosmic-ray composition models, each divided into five mass groups, to calibrate the detector's absolute energy response in the range of 4 - 37 TeV. We quantify the fractional deviation between the calibrated and simulated energy scales by determining a best-fit scale shift parameter of $\epsilon$ =-0.04 $\pm$ 0.03. This yields a 95% confidence interval of -9% to +0.2% for the systematic energy scale deviation. Complementing the simulation based on hadronic interaction model, this geomagnetic calibration provides a data-driven physical validation of the simulated WCDA energy response, effectively bounding systematic uncertainties and refining the overall energy scale.

title: Reconstructing the mass-redshift distribution of supermassive black holes using multiband gravitational-wave observations
authors: Alorika Kar, Souvik Jana, Enrico Barausse, Parameswaran Ajith
abstract: The formation and evolution of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remain major open questions in astrophysics. Astrophysical models of SMBHs invoke black-hole (BH) seeds formed at high redshift, which subsequently grow through gas accretion and mergers. Although observations of high-redshift quasars and active galactic nuclei constrain these scenarios, the mechanisms governing SMBH formation and growth remain uncertain. Future gravitational-wave (GW) observations across the millihertz, decihertz, and audio-frequency bands will provide a complementary and direct probe of SMBH assembly by tracing their merger history. We investigate the extent to which multiband GW observations can reconstruct the mass-redshift distribution of these mergers. We simulate populations of BH mergers predicted by different astrophysical models and identify those observable by the millihertz detector LISA, the decihertz detector LGWA, and next-generation ground-based detectors operating in the audio-frequency band. We reconstruct the mass-redshift distribution of these mergers using the nonparametric inference code FIGARO. We find that combining observations across frequency bands substantially improves the reconstruction for the light-seed models considered here, whose merger populations span broad ranges of mass and redshift. In contrast, for the heavy-seed models considered here, LISA alone recovers most of the accessible mass-redshift distribution, with little additional improvement from the multiband network.

title: Possible origins of the two γ-ray components C0 and C1 in IC 443
authors: Yujun Xian, Huan Yu, Bo Wang, Jun Fang
abstract: Recent LHAASO observations of IC~443 reveal that its high-energy $\gamma$-ray emission can be decomposed into two components with clearly distinct spatial morphologies and spectral properties, namely the compact component C0 and component C1 with an angular extent of 0.67$^\circ$. We aim to explain the $\gamma$-ray emission mechanisms responsible for the two components in IC~443 and to further investigate their respective possible astrophysical counterparts. We model components C0 and C1 independently using two different physical scenarios. For component C0, we adopt an SNR-MC hadronic model that accounts for finite source-size effects to describe the escape and diffusion of high-energy particles and their $\gamma$-ray production via pp interactions with the surrounding molecular clouds. For component C1 , we employ a spatially dependent multi-zone leptonic transport model and describe the evolution of high-energy electrons under the combined action of advection, diffusion, and energy losses using a Fokker--Planck-type equation. The model reproduces the SEDs of components C0 and C1 well. Component C0 exhibits a pronounced $\pi^0$-decay feature, and the maximum energy of its escaping particles reaches the PeV scale. The $\gamma$-ray emission from component C1 can be explained by inverse Compton scattering. Its diffusion coefficient is approximately two orders of magnitude lower than that in the surrounding interstellar medium, and no significant synchrotron counterpart is detected. The $\gamma$-ray emission from IC~443 involves the combined action of multiple physical mechanisms. Component C0 may be a potential PeVatron candidate, whereas component C1 may correspond to a potential TeV halo candidate.

title: Radio emission from a local Little Red Dot: a challenge to the ionized cocoon scenario
authors: Giovanni Mazzolari, Hannah Übler, Grace E.V. Blomfield, Marcella Brusa, Jianhang Chen, Ric Davies, Francesco D'Eugenio, Frank Eisenhauer, Reinhard Genzel, Roberto Gilli, Yannick Gilmer, Shweta Jain, Xihan Ji, Ignas Juodzbalis, Dharam V. Lal, Xiaojing Lin, Roberto Maiolino, Marco Mignoli, Meghana Pannikkote, Eleonora Parlanti, Isabella Prandoni, Karla Rodriguez-Amber, Taro Shimizu, Giulia Tozzi, Bartolomeo Trefoloni
abstract: Several scenarios have been proposed to explain the properties of Little Red Dots (LRDs), invoking either heavy obscuration by dense neutral gas, super-Eddington accretion, or an ionized gas cocoon that produces electron scattering. Radio observations can distinguish between these scenarios. Radio emission is largely unaffected by neutral gas and dust obscuration, whereas free-free absorption can suppress it in the presence of large free electron columns. Here, we investigate the origin of radio emission from the local LRD J1047. We jointly analyze its radio data and the broad H$\alpha$ emission from optical spectroscopy to test the predictions of different physical scenarios. We find that the observed radio luminosity must have an AGN origin, and it is consistent with that of a standard radio-quiet AGN obscured by dense neutral gas. Pure super-Eddington accretion underpredicts the radio luminosity by a factor of $\sim 30$, although a combination of super-Eddington accretion and obscuration remains viable. Interestingly, the statistically preferred model for the H$\alpha$ profile is an exponential fit, which is often associated with electron scattering in LRDs. This interpretation implies an electron column density of $N_e=2.4\times10^{24}\rm~cm^{-2}$ and a strong free-free absorption ($\tau_{\rm ff,5GHz}\sim 10^6$), incompatible with the radio detection. This tension suggests that the exponential profiles of J1047 more likely trace a stratified broad line region rather than electron scattering, with potential implications for virial black-hole mass estimates also in high-$z$ LRDs. Less likely, the radio emission may escape through a partially covering ionized medium or originate outside the putative scattering cocoon.

title: Unveiling the Central Black Hole of NGC 3862: A Direct Mass Determination Using ALMA's High-Resolution Molecular Gas Kinematics
authors: Tuan N. Le, Dieu D. Nguyen, Hai N. Ngo, Elena Gallo, Tinh Q. T. Le, Tien H. T. Ho, Fan Zou, Que T. Le, Huy G. Tong, Huy M. B. Tran
abstract: We present the direct dynamical measurement of the supermassive black hole (SMBH) mass in NGC 3862 (3C 264), a massive Fanaroff-Riley type I radio galaxy. Using ALMA $^{12}$CO(2-1) observations, we map the cold molecular gas kinematics in the circumnuclear disk and model them with the KinMS forward-modeling code. The $^{12}$CO(2-1) disk exhibits a nearly face-on, ring-like morphology with regular disk rotation and a steep central velocity rise, providing clean dynamical constraints on the central gravitational potential. Our best-fit model yields $M_{\rm BH} = 2.40^{+0.52}_{-0.32}[{\rm stat.}] \pm 0.91 [{\rm sys.}] \times 10^9~M_\odot$ and a stellar mass-to-light ratio of $M/L_{\rm F814W} = 4.11^{+0.99}_{-0.27}[{\rm stat.}] \pm 0.17 [{\rm sys.}]~M_\odot/L_\odot$ (both at $1\sigma$ confidence level). This dynamically derived $M/L_{\rm F814W}$ consistent with an old, metal-rich stellar population and a Salpeter IMF. The SMBH sphere of influence is spatially resolved, confirming the robustness of our measurement. This places NGC 3862 among SMBHs with direct molecular gas dynamical constraints, contributing to the census needed to calibrate SMBH-host galaxy co-evolution models at the high-mass end of the scaling relations.

title: Asgard/NOTT: L-band nulling interferometry at the VLTI IV. Prospects for characterising hot exozodiacal dust
authors: Kevin Ollmann, Romain Laugier, Jeremy P. Scott, Thomas A. Stuber, Steve Ertel, Denis Defrere, Florian Kirchschlager, Olivier Absil, Germain Garreau, Jean-Charles Augereau, William Danchi, Tim D. Pearce, Sebastian Wolf
abstract: Near-infrared interferometric surveys have revealed extended emission around the photosphere of $\approx 40$ main-sequence stars, attributed to the presence of hot exozodiacal dust (HEZD). A promising technique for investigating this phenomenon is nulling interferometry. The Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) nulling interferometer NOTT (Nulling Observations of exoplaneTs and dusT) is designed to characterise exoplanets and HEZD in the $L'$ band ($3.5-4.0\,\mu$m). We aim to assess NOTT's potential for the detection and characterisation of HEZD with various instrumental and model parameter configurations. We model the HEZD as an optically thin dust ring, using the nearby Sun-like star $\tau$ Ceti with HEZD as a reference model. Applying the end-to-end nulling tool SCIFYsim to model the instrumental response of NOTT to simulated HEZD brightness distributions, we evaluate how variations in HEZD and instrumental parameters affect NOTT's key observables: the photon flux rate and the null depth. We demonstrate that NOTT is capable of disentangling stellar and dust contributions to the signal and detecting HEZD. The null depth and photon flux rate are sensitive to the HEZD geometry, with inclination, position angle, and ring location having the strongest impact on the signal. Although the detailed temporal signatures are target-specific, the results can be generalised to other systems. NOTT has the potential to deliver unprecedented sensitivity for HEZD observations, granting access to detailed information through spectral dispersion, beam-combination schemes, and exploitation of sky rotation. This enables more sensitive HEZD detections than is possible with current instruments, and improved spatial constraints on the dust, as well as variability studies.

title: Analytical formulae for planet-planet or moon-moon tides
authors: Michaela Walterová, Marie Běhounková
abstract: Almost negligible among the solar system planets, mutual tides raised by a secondary on another secondary orbiting the same primary may gain increased importance in tightly packed systems, e.g., between the components of close-in exoplanetary systems or between the moons of gas giants. In this work, we derive an analytical formula for the planet-planet tidal potential and for the effect of mutual tides on the rotational and orbital evolution of moons or planets in a coplanar configuration. The procedure follows closely the steps of W. M. Kaula (1961), and the resulting potential and derived quantities are presented in the form of an expansion into modes of different frequencies (in the temporal domain) and spherical harmonic components (in the spatial domain). The analytical formulae are implemented into a code and compared with an independent numerical solution.

title: A lepto-hadronic perspective on the properties of the candidate neutrino-emitter blazar 5BZQ J0808+4950
authors: Margot Boughelilba, Leonard Pfeiffer, Jose Maria Sanchez Zaballa, Alessandra Azzollini, Annette Bremer, Sara Buson, Massimiliano Lincetto
abstract: The role of active galactic nuclei in the production of high-energy neutrinos has been highlighted by the association of the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 with IceCube neutrino events. In particular, blazars, with their powerful jets, are potential sites of neutrino production via (photo-)hadronic interactions. The gamma-ray bright blazar 5BZQJ0808+4950 is consistent with a spatial anisotropy in the IceCube neutrino all-sky maps. An individual high-energy neutrino event, IC110929A, was also reported in the direction of this blazar. Although the correlation between the gamma-ray bright blazars and the neutrino production remains inconclusive, 5BZQ J0808+4950, with a luminous accretion disk serving as a photon field for the photo-hadronic interactions, offers the opportunity to test the relation between neutrino production and the radiative output of the blazar jet. We compile available multi-wavelength data and analyze the gamma-ray light curve of 5BZQ J0808+4950, leading us to define six contemporaneous epochs to model the source's spectral energy distribution and its evolution over time. We use a lepto-hadronic, time-dependent framework to model 5BZQ J0808+4950, taking into account external photon fields. We find that the solutions corresponding to the different states the source exhibits are explained mostly by a change in the particles' injection properties. The correlation between the predicted X-ray and the neutrino luminosity in this source is stronger than the correlation between gamma-ray and neutrino luminosity. We predict that the rate of neutrinos detectable by IceCube for this blazar ranges from $\sim 10^{-3}$ to $\sim10^{-1}$ neutrinos per epoch. Assuming Poisson statistics, the predicted neutrino number contemporaneous with the interval in which the high-energy neutrino event IC110929A was detected, is compatible with the detection of one neutrino.

title: Sun-like stars show lowered X-ray activity together with over-rotation at beyond-solar ages
authors: K. Poppenhaeger, N. Ilić, J. van Saders, J. D. Alvarado-Gómez, F. Anders, M. M. Jardine, A. Warmuth, E. M. Amazo-Gómez, S. A. Barnes
abstract: In recent years, substructure in the age-rotation relationship of cool, sun-like stars has been identified, showing deviations from the historical Skumanich law. Since magnetic activity is expected to be the physical root cause of the stellar spin-down, namely via the magnetic braking process mediated through stellar winds, changes in spin-down should correspond to unusual activity behaviour. We selected a sample of old sun-like stars in the solar neighborhood with asteroseismic age estimates and measured rotation periods, and present an analysis of their magnetic activity using deep X-ray observations from XMM-Newton. We observe that sample stars less massive than the Sun (late-G and early-K) agree well with the established rotation-activity relationship, while early-G and late-F stars with masses above solar tend to be unusually X-ray dim for their rotation period. The latter stars rotate faster than same-colour stars in the solar-age open cluster M67, despite being older than M67. Those stars are characterized by either low metallicity ([Fe/H]$\approx -0.2$ dex compared to solar) or by a mix of low coronal temperatures ($< 1.5$ million K) and very low X-ray surface fluxes ($\lesssim 10^4$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$). We conclude that there is sufficient dynamo activity for coronal emission in the sample stars, since we successfully detect the majority of them in our X-ray observations. We argue that stars with extremely low coronal temperature and/or low X-ray flux through the stellar surface may produce an inefficient spin-down through hampered angular momentum shedding. If this is indeed the cause for their over-rotation, the onset age of this effect would need to be at an age of approximately 3~Gyr. However, this behaviour is at odds with studies of stars in the open cluster M67 with a cluster age of $\sim4$ Gyr, which do not show a faster-rotating population of sun-like stars.
comments: Accepted for publication by Astronomy & Astrophysics

figs.cap: Comparison of fundamental stellar parameters of the sample stars from various sources (DR3-GSP = GSP values from Gaia Collaboration et al. 2023, B16 = Brewer et al. 2016, N17 = Nissen et al. 2017, B15 = Buchhave and Latham 2015, H21 = Hall et al. 2021, M24 = Metcalfe et al. 2024). (2020) and Gruner et al. (2023); solid grey lines are iso-colour lines. To guide the eye, we have plotted the colour-rotation sequence of M67 again at an age of 11 Gyrs, to make it easier to discern whether the sample stars sit below or above the plane indicated by the dashed iso-colour lines. We colour-code the sample stars by their deviation from the plane, with red circles sitting at longer rotation periods above the plane and blue squares at shorter rotation periods below the plane. The majority of the sample stars spin faster than stars of the same $(BP-RP)_{0}$ colour in M67.

The original rotation-activity relationship fit to the W11 sample from Reiners et al. (2014) is shown as the dashed grey line, our orthogonal distance fit to the same W11 data is the solid black line. Our target stars cover a wide band of activity levels, and about half of our sample stars cluster along or even below the extreme low-activity edge of the W11 sample (stars 1, 2, 4, and 8).

Several properties of the sample stars shown as a function of each star’s distance to the canonical rotation-activity relationship from Fig. 6. Due to the limited sample size, the potential trends discussed in the text are to be taken as suggestive, but not as statistically significant. Top panel: The stars that rotate faster than their counterparts in M67 despite being older are also the ones that are located farthest below the rotation-activity relationship. Middle panel: For the stars where we could constrain coronal temperatures, there is potentially a trend of decreasing coronal temperature with stronger disagreement to the rotation-activity relationship, if star 1 is an outlier. Bottom panel: Three stars show significantly sub-solar metallicity ($\lesssim 0.1$ dex, triangle symbols); those are the stars we did not detect in X-rays and were only able to derive upper limits on their X-ray luminosity for.

title: Powerful Radio Jets and Galaxy Assembly Align at Cosmic Noon
authors: Peter Breiding, Marco Chiaberge, Eileen T. Meyer, Bryan Hilbert, Mojegan Azadi, Stefi A. Baum, Martin Haas, George Miley, Christopher P. O'Dea, Eric S. Perlman, Belinda Wilkes, S. P. Willner, Colin Norman
abstract: Powerful radio galaxies at cosmic noon ($1<z<2$) offer a unique laboratory for investigating jet-driven supermassive black hole (SMBH) feedback on their host galaxies and surrounding environments. Unlike broad-lined quasars, radio galaxies lack a dominant nuclear point source in the rest-frame optical--UV, enabling direct constraints on host-galaxy structure and its relation to the radio jet. We analyze Hubble Space Telescope (HST) WFC3/IR (rest-frame optical) and WFC3/UVIS (rest-frame UV) imaging of the $z>1$ 3CR radio galaxies. Beyond confirming the classical rest-frame UV alignment effect, we find that the radio jets preferentially align with the major axes of the smooth rest-frame optical hosts, extending the alignment to the older stellar component. The projected axes of candidate mergers in eight systems preferentially follow the radio axes. This multiscale coherence suggests a common projected axis linking the radio source to host assembly, perhaps established by repeated mergers or anisotropic infall. We test scattered quasar light and jet-triggered star formation as origins of the UV emission along this axis. The much shallower-than-expected radial decline in UV surface brightness disfavors simple scattering as the dominant population-wide origin, while ionized-gas masses further disfavor electron scattering. The required dust masses are small relative to global reservoirs, so dust scattering remains feasible in individual regions. Comparing stellar-population ages and jet-propagation times, we identify seven UV-emitting regions as strong candidates for recently initiated jet-triggered star formation. Together, these alignments reveal an assembly-linked direction along which jets may shock or compress material and hidden-quasar radiation may illuminate it.
comments: 38 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal

title: Solid-state formation of H$_2$CS and CH$_3$SH in molecular clouds: Carbon-initiated reactions with atomic and molecular hydrogen
authors: F. Kruczkiewicz, J. C. Santos, G. Fedoseev, S. Ioppolo, C. M. R. Rocha, K.-J. Chuang
abstract: The solid-state formation pathways of thioformaldehyde (H$_2$CS) and methanethiol (CH$_3$SH) in dense molecular clouds remain poorly constrained. We investigate carbon-initiated reactions in hydrogen sulfide (H$_2$S) ice in the presence of atomic or molecular hydrogen. We co-deposited H$_2$S, ground-state atomic carbon, and H or H$_2$ at 10 K under ultra-high vacuum. We monitored the reaction products using reflection absorption infrared spectroscopy (RAIRS) and characterized their thermal desorption using temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) with quadrupole mass spectrometry. Gas-phase ab initio calculations were used to assess pathways to CH$_3$SH formation. Atomic carbon reacted with H$_2$S at 10 K to form H$_2$CS, detected as both monomers and H$_2$CS-derived oligomers. With atomic H, successive H addition to H$_2$CS leads to CH$_3$SH. With molecular H$_2$, CH$_3$SH also forms efficiently. The results support an alternative pathway in which C reacts with H$_2$ to form CH$_2$, which abstracts H from H$_2$S. The resulting CH$_3$ and SH radicals can then recombine to form CH$_3$SH. The infrared bands and TPD fragmentation patterns support the formation of H$_2$CS and CH$_3$SH in the ice at 10 K. These findings expand the set of viable solid-state pathways to sulfur-bearing molecules and constrain models of sulfur chemistry in prestellar environments.
comments: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics. 13 pages, 7 figures, including Appendix A

title: Cosmological structure formation in ultralight dark matter
authors: K. Korshynska, A. I. Yakimenko, Y. Revaz, E. V. Gorbar
abstract: An important challenge in cosmology is to describe the formation of galaxies and structures, starting from small inhomogeneities in the early Universe, which later grew and formed the so- called dark matter halos. We consider the dark matter to be composed of ultralight bosons and simplify the general complex problem of halo formation by using the time-dependent variational analysis approach. This yields, for the first time, a fully analytical equation for the time-evolution of perturbations towards isolated haloes. We follow the evolution of the halo size and density during different stages of its formation, revealing the role of the background density, Universe expansion, and quantum pressure.

title: Welopō'ai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun
authors: Étienne Artigau, Charles-Antoine Parent, Atanas K. Stefanov, Érika Le Bourdais, Souleymane Ouedraogo, Alexandrine L'Heureux, Patrick Dufour, René Doyon, Neil J. Cook, Charles Cadieux, Clémence Fontanive, Luc Arnold, Jean-François Donati, Matthias R. Schreiber, Ryan Cloutier, Xavier Delfosse, Céline Reylé, Thierry Forveille, Tianqi Cang, Claire Moutou, Alexandre C. M. Correia
abstract: Context. We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf companion to the M4 V dwarf Welopo'ai Aa (IRAS 21500+5903) during a radial-velocity search for exoplanets with SPIRou. The system is located at 8.46 pc and forms a hierarchical triple with a more distant white dwarf, which has no known analogue within 30 pc. Aims. We characterise the orbital architecture and component masses through a joint Keplerian fit of radial velocities and astrometry, derive the physical parameters of the M dwarf and both white dwarfs, and discuss the implications for common-envelope evolution and hierarchical triple dynamics. Methods. We obtained radial velocity measurements with SPIRou spread over 4.8 yr, revealing a large-amplitude signal ($\sim$16 km/s peak-to-peak) that is inconsistent with planetary companions. Follow-up speckle imaging with 'Alopeke at Gemini North and near-infrared (NIR) imaging with GNIRS confirmed a white dwarf companion at sub-arcsecond separation. Results. The system comprises an inner binary with a semi-major axis of $4.644 \pm 0.017$ au ($P \approx 9.83$ yr), consisting of the primary M4 V ($M = 0.4189^{+0.0073}_{-0.0072} M_\odot$) and a white dwarf companion ($M = 0.6180^{+0.0046}_{-0.0045} M_\odot$, $T_{\rm eff} \sim 5210 \pm 320$ K, cooling age 5.3-5.5 Gyr). This inner pair lies at a projected separation of 123.9 au ($P > 1000$ yr) from a previously known white dwarf. The dynamically determined mass of the inner white dwarf is one of only a handful of such measurements for white dwarfs within 20 pc, and the most precise, at the sub-percent (0.7%) level. Conclusions. This system is the closest known triple containing multiple white dwarfs and offers direct dynamical constraints on common-envelope evolution and hierarchical triple stability. Furthermore, a tentative near-infrared (IR) excess towards the inner white dwarf further hints at circumstellar dust.
comments: 22 pages, 12 figures, 10 tables. Published in A&A

title: Interpretable attention-based neural posterior estimation for fast radio burst cosmology
authors: Tian-Yang Sun, Ji-Guo Zhang, Wan-Peng Sun, Jing-Fei Zhang, Xin Zhang
abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) probe the integrated free-electron density along extragalactic sightlines and can be used to study late-time cosmic evolution. Conventional Bayesian analyses require repeated evaluations of computationally expensive likelihoods, making inference increasingly challenging as FRB catalogs grow. In this work, we develop an interpretable attention-based neural posterior estimator (AttNPE) for rapid posterior inference of the physical parameters from FRB catalogs with measured redshifts. The attention encoder compresses the catalog into a low-dimensional representation, and a conditional masked autoregressive flow maps samples from a base distribution to the seven-dimensional posterior. AttNPE yields posterior distributions in close agreement with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), recovering the parameter correlations in both simulated and observed FRB catalogs. For the observed catalog, AttNPE generates $5\times10^4$ posterior samples in $0.036$~s after training, compared with $72.8$~h for the reference MCMC run, giving an elapsed-time ratio of $O(10^6)$. The attention-weight analysis shows that intermediate-redshift FRBs ($0.3\leq z<0.7$) account for the largest share of the total attention averaged over simulated catalogs following the observed redshift distribution, consistent with the combined influence of source abundance and redshift-dependent sensitivity. These results demonstrate the potential of interpretable neural posterior estimation for efficient and repeated inference in FRB cosmology.
comments: 14 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables

title: Characterization of the $b$-anisotropy for axisymmetric early-type galaxies in TNG50
authors: L. De Deo, A. Gebek, M. Baes, L. Ciotti, S. Pellegrini
abstract: High-quality observations reveal that internal dynamics of axisymmetric ETGs can be more complicated than commonly adopted in modelizations based on the Jeans equations (JEs), with the identity of the radial and vertical velocity dispersions. A well known generalization is obtained by solving the JEs with the prescription of a proportionality factor $b$ between the radial and vertical velocity dispersions; in its simplest form $b$ is assumed constant, while in recent studies $b=b(z)$. We investigate the properties of the $b$ parameter and of the other kinematical decomposition parameters commonly adopted in modeling in a sample of ETGs taken from the high-resolution cosmological simulations TNG50. From a selection of highly axisymmetric and passive TNG50 (satellite and central) galaxies at equilibrium, we recovered the maps of $b(R,z)$ and of other important kinematic quantities entering the JEs. In all the selected galaxies the only significantly non-zero velocity streaming component is the azimuthal one, and the velocity dispersion tensor is cylindrically aligned. The maps of $b$ are clearly not constant, and not stratified over planes, instead they present a common structure, with the largest values values near the center, and a wedge structure at large (cylindrical) radii. A phenomenological formula for $b(R,z)$ to be used in applications is proposed. Also the other decomposition parameters are non-constant. No significant differences are found as a function of galaxy flattening and mass, while some difference is observed between satellite and central galaxies. The internal dynamics of the TNG50 galaxies present interesting regularities, worth of investigation. On the other hand, in Jeans based studies of real galaxies some simple assumptions for the choice of anisotropy and kinematical decomposition parameters do not seem appropriate. [abridged]

title: Computation of complex dust grain optical properties: Optimisation method by equivalent representation (OMER)
authors: M.-A. Carpine, N. Ysard, A. Maury
abstract: Computing the optical properties of dust grains is important for understanding various astrophysical environments. However, the numerical methods used to compute these properties require significant computing resources for irregularly shaped or inhomogeneous particles that are representative of realistic grown dust. This study aims to provide an efficient yet accurate Discrete dipole approximation (DDA) computation method for large aggregates with 'complex' monomers and structural details or compositional inhomogeneities. We propose the optimisation method by equivalent representation (OMER) method, which uses optimisation of the optical properties of a known monomer to find an equivalent homogeneous sphere. This sphere can then be used as a substitute for the complex monomer in large aggregates. The method provides a good approximation of complex monomers, as demonstrated in test cases involving large aggregates. Compared to existing methods, OMER shows greater accuracy, particularly in the range from visible to submillimetre wavelengths. The gain in computing time depends on the grain but can exceed two orders of magnitude. The proposed method provides a fast and accurate approximation for estimating the optical properties of materials with complex shapes and paves the way for efficient computation cross-sections for complex dust grain aggregates with thin core-mantle structures or hierarchical aggregates of large sizes.
comments: Accepted for publication in A&A

title: Gaia Science Alerts microlensing events with mass estimates verifiable in Gaia Data Release 4
authors: M. Wicker, Ł. Wyrzykowski, M. Hundertmark, K. Kruszyńska, E. Bachelet, P. Zieliński, M. Kalicki, K. Kotysz, P. J. Mikołajczyk, M. Gromadzki, K. Howil, J. Majumdar, N. Ihanec, M. Nagai, K. Nunota, R. Ogawa, R. Oishi, H. Ose, G. Olmschenk, C. Ranc, N. J. Rattenbury, Y. K. Satoh, T. Sumi, D. Suzuki, T. Tamaoki, S. K. Terry, C. Ueda, P. J. Tristram, A. Vandorou, H. Yama
abstract: Gaia Science Alerts provide an all-sky stream of photometric transients, including events consistent with gravitational microlensing. For such events, forthcoming epoch astrometry from the Gaia mission offers the possibility of testing photometric lens mass predictions. While microlensing parallax inferred from the photometric light curve can constrain the event geometry, a direct lens mass measurement additionally requires the angular Einstein radius, which may be accessible through astrometric microlensing. We aim to construct a pre-Data-Release-4 (DR4) sample of Gaia microlensing events for which the available photometry provides a measurable microlensing-parallax signal. This allows us to derive statistical predictions for the lens mass and distance. We forward-modelled these events to predict the detectability of the astrometric microlensing signal in Gaia DR4. We identify 56 Gaia Science Alerts microlensing events with 71 point-source point-lens solutions with annual parallaxes that satisfy our fit-quality, posterior-boundedness, and parallax-significance criteria. Lens masses and distances were inferred using two prior-based frameworks, pyLIMASS and the Besançon Galaxy Model, which combine the measured microlensing parameters and Gaia source information with stellar-population and Galactic models. These inferred parameters were used to simulate Gaia DR4-like along-scan astrometry and estimate the detectability of the astrometric microlensing signal. The inferred lens masses and distances remain strongly prior-dependent without a direct angular Einstein radius measurement. Among the 284 event-solution-prior branches, 47 are classified as high-confidence astrometric detections using Gaia DR4-like simulations. These predictions can be tested once epoch astrometry is released in Gaia DR4.
comments: 17 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in Sect. 11. Celestial mechanics and astrometry of Astronomy & Astrophysics on 16 October 2026

title: Cosmological First-Order Phase Transitions with Full Nonlinear Gravity
authors: Campbell Benedix, Eve Currens, John T. Giblin Jr, Chloe Richards
abstract: Cosmological first-order phase transitions can contribute to the stochastic gravitational wave background. For decades, these first-order phase transitions have been studied using a Friedmann--Lemaître--Robertson--Walker background where the gravitational waves are treated as linear perturbations. Here, we present simulations of a first-order phase transition in the presence of fully nonlinear general relativity, using the BSSN formalism. We simulate a universe that contains a scalar field alongside a relativistic radiation fluid. We focus on GUT-scale transitions in which bubbles nucleate near the horizon size. We describe a method to construct initial data that satisfies the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints, starting from a Coleman--de~Luccia-like bubble profile and adjusting the bubble radius. We compute the gravitational wave spectrum directly from the trace-free extrinsic curvature and find a present-day peak amplitude of $\Omega_{\rm GW,0}h^2 \sim 5\times 10^{-11}$, consistent with earlier results that do not include nonlinear gravity. The peak frequency depends on the symmetry-breaking scale and could fall anywhere from the LISA band to GHz frequencies. At late times, the field fragments into long-lived oscillons, which push its effective equation of state toward that of matter.

title: JCMT POL-2 observations of NGC 253: evidence for large-scale reordering of magnetic fields in giant molecular cloud complexes
authors: Kate Pattle, Walter K. Gear
abstract: In this paper we present observations of the magnetic field of the starburst galaxy NGC 253 made in polarized 850 $\mu$m dust emission using the POL-2 polarimeter on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT). While the magnetic field typically traces the galactic spiral structure, we see significant deviations in field direction associated with the presence of stellar and/or supernova feedback, with the mean plane-of-sky magnetic field direction offset 24$^{\circ}$ from the galactic plane. Polarization fraction is anticorrelated with total 850 $\mu$m intensity, with a power-law index of 0.72$\pm$0.03. Using the Fasano-Franceschini test, we find that the positions of POL-2 detections and radio sources in the spiral arms are inconsistent with one another, indicative of depolarization resulting from magnetic fields being tangled on scales smaller than the 240 pc JCMT 850 $\mu$m beam in sites of star formation and feedback. Moreover, in both the starburst superwind and in one star-forming clump in the spiral arms, we observe a magnetic field direction consistent with being directed out of the plane of the galaxy. We thus hypothesise that magnetic fields in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) of NGC 253 are undergoing an evolutionary sequence from a relatively ordered field parallel to the spiral arms in the pre-star-formation gas, to a complex field caused by the interplay of turbulence, gravity and small-scale feedback in relatively young GMCs, to a field that is reordered out of the plane of the galaxy as large-scale HII region expansion reshapes the gas and dust of galactic spiral arms.
comments: 14 pages, 12 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in MNRAS

title: A $10^5\,M_\odot$ Black Hole in the Bulgeless Spiral Galaxy IC 342: First Stellar-Dynamical $M_{\rm BH}$ Measurement with Keck/OSIRIS LGS-AO
authors: Tuan N. Le, Dieu D. Nguyen, Mark Durré, Alister W. Graham, Elena Gallo, Hai N. Ngo, Tien H. T. Ho, Tinh Q. T. Le, Thiem Hoang, Igor V. Chilingarian, Roberto Soria, Fan Zou, Huy G. Tong, Que T. Le, Huy M. B. Tran
abstract: We present the first direct stellar-dynamical measurement of an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in IC 342, a nearby nearly face-on ($i\approx31^\circ$) bulgeless spiral at $D=3.45\pm0.13$ Mpc, using near-infrared integral-field spectroscopy with Keck/OSIRIS LGS-AO. The heavy foreground extinction ($A_{\mathrm{F814W}}\approx0.74$ mag) renders the nucleus inaccessible to optical spectroscopy, making $K$-band observations at $\sim$2.3 $\mu$m the only viable path to high-resolution nuclear kinematics. Two-dimensional stellar kinematics extracted from the CO bandheads via pPXF at $0.062''$ resolution reveal a central velocity dispersion rising from $\sim$42 km s$^{-1}$ at $r\gtrsim0.2''$ to a peak of $\sim$49 km s$^{-1}$, providing kinematic evidence for a central dark mass within the nuclear star cluster (NSC; $M_\mathrm{NSC}\approx1.17\times10^7~M_\odot$). Modeling these kinematics with an ensemble of four JAM models, spanning cylindrical and spherical velocity-ellipsoid alignments and two PSF representations, combined with an MGE mass model constructed from a three-Sérsic plus exponential-disk decomposition of archival HST/WFC3 F814W imaging and incorporating a physically motivated stellar mass-to-light ratio gradient, driven by the young central NSC population, yields $M_\mathrm{BH}=(1.95\pm0.61)\times10^5~M_\odot$. Accounting for this stellar population gradient is essential for the detection: standard constant-$M/L$ models systematically overestimate the central stellar mass, hiding the BH signature and yielding only an upper limit. The stellar orbits are near-isotropic ($\beta\approx0$), typical of fast-rotating late-type spirals. This measurement places IC 342 among the rare bulgeless spirals with a direct dynamical $M_{\rm BH}$ at the IMBH mass scale, where both the NSC and BH are directly characterized, providing a new anchor for compact massive object co-evolution models.
comments: 26 pages, 14 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to ApJ

title: The infrared arc around $α$ Crucis: a weak interaction with a structured interstellar medium
authors: Naira Azatyan, Elena Nikoghosyan, Marine Torosyan, Haik Harutyunian, Derenik Andreasyan, Vardges Grigoryan, Arman Khachatryan, Anahit Samsonyan
abstract: Infrared arc-shaped structures around early-type stars are commonly interpreted as stellar wind bow shocks, although their morphology may also be shaped by gas motions and density variations in the surrounding interstellar medium. We present a multiwavelength study of the infrared arc associated with the nearby $\alpha$ Crucis system, comprising HD 108248 (B0.5 IV), HD 108249 (B1 V), and HD 108250 (B4 V). We combine WISE, Herschel, Planck, stellar astrometry, and eROSITA X-ray data to investigate the structure and its relation to the stellar components. The WISE W4 ridge extends over $\sim$0.65 pc and has a median PSF-corrected width of $\sim$0.037 pc. The HD 108248/HD 108249 pair lies $\sim$0.13 pc from the ridge, compared with $\sim$0.17 pc for HD 108250. Relative to the mean motion of the Lower Centaurus-Crux (LCC) subgroup of the Scorpius-Centaurus association, the close pair is consistent with LCC, whereas HD 108250 has a transverse peculiar velocity of only $\sim$1.8 km s$^{-1}$. Its motion lies within $\sim$23$^\circ$ of the geometrical symmetry axis of the infrared arc, but points in the opposite sense from the arc. Herschel maps show slightly higher median dust temperature ($\Delta T_d\sim$0.8 K) and molecular-hydrogen column density ($\Delta N_{\rm H2}\sim$7$\times$10$^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$) toward the W4-defined region than in the nearby background. On larger scales, Planck maps reveal a strongly structured microwave environment around the system. Both the HD 108248/HD 108249 pair and HD 108250 are detected by eROSITA, with the former approximately 60 times more luminous in X-rays. The combined morphology, kinematics, and dust properties do not support an unambiguous classical high-velocity bow-shock interpretation. Instead, the arc likely traces a weak interaction between the multiple stellar system and an inhomogeneous ambient medium.
comments: Accepted for publication in Astrophysics and Space Science

title: Thermodynamics of gas giants accreting via shocks: the role of molecular hydrogen dissociation
authors: Bingjie Zha, Zhuo Chen
abstract: Within the core-accretion framework, gas giants acquire most of their mass through accretion shocks during runaway gas accretion. The shock thermodynamics---governed by radiative cooling, accretion history, and equation of state (EoS)---sets the post-shock gas entropy and initial thermal state, strongly influencing both observables and subsequent evolution. We aim to build a coupled evolutionary model predicting the initial thermodynamic conditions, intrinsic luminosities, and upper limits on magnetic field strengths of gas giants across diverse accretion histories. We couple radiation hydrodynamics and $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociation to long-term planetary interior evolution by training a physics-informed neural network (PINN) predictor on 1000 first-principles simulations resolving the shock physics. This PINN provides post-shock outer boundary conditions for MESA to evolve the planetary envelope beyond runaway accretion. The PINN predicts higher post-shock temperatures than the canonical cold-start model, with the discrepancy widening with planetary mass, while post-shock entropy jumps sharply when $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociates at $\sim 2000$ K. Gas giants evolved with PINN-derived boundary conditions achieve intrinsic luminosities 4--10 times higher than cold-start models. Under optimistic assumptions, the maximum magnetic field strength at $2 R_{\mathrm{J}}$ reaches a few gauss for a $0.3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$ planet, $\sim 100$ G for $1 M_{\mathrm{J}}$, and $\sim 500$ G for $3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$. Incorporating detailed radiation hydrodynamics and realistic thermodynamics into accretion shock models yields higher initial entropies, brighter intrinsic luminosities, and stronger magnetic fields, providing improved constraints on the masses and accretion rates of directly imaged exoplanets.
comments: submitted to A&A, comments welcome

title: Early spectra of AT2017gfo from scaled 3D merger ejecta: mass--velocity distribution, 3D structure, and treatment of line opacity
authors: Luke J. Shingles, Christine E. Collins, Vimal Vijayan, Andreas Flörs, Oliver Just, Fiona McNeill, Gerrit Leck, Andreas Bauswein, Gabriel Martínez-Pinedo, Stuart A. Sim
abstract: We present ARTIS radiative transfer calculations for neutron star merger ejecta with line-by-line opacities, wavelength-calibrated lanthanide data, and time-dependent r-process compositions and thermalisation, testing how the early kilonova depends on the mass-velocity distribution, dimensionality, and line treatment. We rescale 3D dynamical ejecta from a merger simulation in density and velocity to approximate AT2017gfo. Mass scaling alone provides good agreement with the bolometric light curve but inconsistent spectra. With velocities additionally halved, the model also reproduces the observed spectra at 1.4, 2.4, and (albeit less accurately) 3.4 days. The Sr II triplet contributes most to the 10500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ peak, and La III and Gd III to the 13500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ shoulder. Although hydrodynamically not fully self-consistent, this model is to our knowledge the first kilonova model based on calibrated atomic data that reproduces the light curve and main spectral features of the early AT2017gfo, suggesting that total (dynamical plus post-merger) ejecta with higher mass, lower velocity, and similar composition compared to our dynamical ejecta could explain AT2017gfo. A 2D azimuthal average mixes lanthanide-poor with lanthanide-rich regions, smooths the density, and makes the averaged model three times fainter at 1 day and redder throughout than the 3D model, highlighting the importance of 3D modelling. We compare the line-by-line macroatom treatment with expansion-opacity and line-binned schemes with thermal redistribution, using identical atomic data. Luminosities agree to $\lesssim 10$ per cent after 1 day, but the expansion-opacity scheme, unlike converged line-binned schemes, overestimates the spectral flux by up to 20 per cent, which can bias inferred abundances.
comments: 22 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to MNRAS

title: The Gas-Phase Metallicity and Nitrogen abundances in typical galaxies at $z\sim5$
authors: Claudia Di Cesare, Gauri Kotiwale, Jorryt Matthee, Alice Shapley, Alba Covelo-Paz, Kasper E. Heintz, Pascal A. Oesch, Edoardo Iani, Anna Frebel, Daichi Kashino, Ivan G. Kramarenko, Sara Mascia, Rohan P. Naidu, Irene Shivaei, Alberto Torralba, Rongmon Bordoloi, Emma Giovinazzo, Jasleen Matharu
abstract: The relation between stellar mass and gas-phase metallicity (MZR) is a key tracer of the baryon cycle in galaxies. JWST now gives access to rest-optical emission lines at z > 3, enabling unprecedented constraints on the chemical enrichment and the conditions of the interstellar medium of galaxies in the early Universe. In this work, we present the MZR at $z=3.8-6.6$ from stacked NIRCam/grism spectra of 1748 H$\alpha$-selected star-forming galaxies compiled over an area of 320 arcmin$^2$. The simple H$\alpha$ flux-limited selection allows us to measure representative [NII]$\lambda$6584/H$\alpha$ and [SII]$\lambda\lambda$6716,6731/ H$\alpha$ ratios in stacks spanning $\rm log(M_\star/M_\odot)=8-10.2$, extending the upper mass range of previous high-redshift MZR measurements by $\sim1$ dex. Gas-phase metallicities are derived from these ratios using strong-line calibrations recently derived from high-redshift galaxies. The[NII]-based MZR has a slope $\gamma = 0.42^{+0.10}_{-0.07}$ and $12+\rm log(O/H) = 7.94^{+0.06}_{-0.09}$ at $\rm log(M_\star/M_\odot) = 9$, in broad agreement with recent empirical studies and hydrodynamical simulations. The [SII]-based relation yields a consistent slope and a $\sim0.3$ dex higher normalization, within the systematic uncertainties of strong-line calibrations. From the resolved [SII] doublet we infer a median electron density of $n_e = 184^{+226}_{-169}\,\rm cm^{-3}$. Combining [NII] and [SII], we indirectly estimate the N/O ratio and find that it follows the trend expected from primary and secondary nitrogen production, with no evidence for nitrogen enhancement in the HII region emission that dominates our galaxies. Our results provide a benchmark for the chemical enrichment and ISM conditions of typical star-forming galaxies at $z\sim5$ across a wide mass range.
comments: Main text 16 pages, 8 figures. Main results in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6. Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome

title: Stratonovich approximation for halo bias: An efficient framework within excursion set theory
authors: Milad Noorikuhani, Shant Baghram
abstract: We develop an efficient framework for calculating halo multiplicity functions and bias parameters in the excursion-set approach based on the previously presented Hertz and Stratonovich approximations for the first-crossing distribution. The framework enables efficient evaluation of first-crossing distributions for a broad class of moving barriers and filter functions, from which halo biases can be calculated within the peak-background split formalism. We compare halo multiplicity functions and biases obtained from these approximations with those computed from first-crossing distributions obtained from numerically generated ensembles of excursion-set trajectories. We find close agreement between predictions based on the Stratonovich approximation and numerical results across a range of barrier parameters and filter choices, demonstrating that the approximation captures the impact of non-Markovian correlations on first-crossing statistics while substantially reducing the computational cost compared to trajectory-based calculations. Overall, this framework provides a flexible and computationally efficient tool for analyzing halo statistics in cosmological applications.
comments: 12 pages, 4 figures. Comments are welcome

title: Investigating the Impact of SAX J1808.4-3658's Very Bright Thermonuclear X-ray Burst on the Accretion Disc with NICER
authors: A. C. Albayati, D. Altamirano, A. Beri, T. Boztepe, D. J. K. Buisson, T. Güver, G. K. Jaisawal, C. Malacaria, M. Ng, A. Sanna, T. E. Strohmayer
abstract: We analyse a bright thermonuclear X-ray burst from the accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar (AMXP) SAX J1808.4-3658, the brightest burst detected by \textit{NICER} to date, to explore interactions between thermonuclear burst radiation and the accretion disc. This burst features a remarkable soft (<1.5 keV) excess in its spectra. For the first time, we simultaneously detect a reflection signal and the signature of an evolving persistent component, with our fits producing a peak persistent scaling factor $f_{a,1} = 59.6\pm0.6$. We find a high peak reflection fraction ($f_{r,1} = 0.82\pm0.15$) and a peak bolometric burst blackbody flux below Eddington (0.68$L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$) despite signatures of photospheric radius expansion. We detect a raised $N_\mathrm{H}$ ($\approx$34% above persistent emission) and raised disc blackbody temperature ($\approx$15% above persistent emission) during the burst's tail. This is the first time that spectroscopic evidence consistent with burst-induced disc heating has been found. We interpret that disc heating could cause the disc to puff up and inhibit burst photons, explaining the high reflection fraction and below-Eddington burst luminosity during the burst peak. We find an increasing count rate starting from $\approx$150s before the burst onset. Spectral analysis revealed a thermal component that evolves towards hotter temperatures closer to the onset of the burst. This is the second detection of this phenomenon from an AMXP. Lastly, we find that both the double-peaked structure and the "pause" in the rise are energy-dependent.
comments: 22 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS

title: Towards modelling redshift uncertainties in the photometric void size function
authors: Pierre Boccard, Giovanni Verza, Giulia Degni, Nico Schuster, Gideon McFarland, Katayoon Ghaemi, Pauline Vielzeuf, Alice Pisani
abstract: We present an extension of the theoretical formalism for the Void Size Function (VSF) to incorporate photometric redshift uncertainties, combining the excursion set with the theory of Lagrangian density peaks. Photometric redshift scatter induces anisotropic line-of-sight smoothing of the density field, which modifies the variance of the field and suppresses the abundance of large voids. We model this effect by damping the variance of the smoothed density field in the theoretical model, and we test it on AbacusSummit halo lightcones with true redshifts and with mock photometric redshifts generated with a Gaussian scatter. The predicted damping of the variance agrees with the one measured in the halo distribution to 1% and the suppression of the VSF due to photometric redshift scatter is well reproduced by the modified model, with recalibrated barrier parameters, for sigma_z <= 0.015 and for voids larger than 40 Mpc/h (about 2.5 mean tracer separations). This work is a first step towards modelling the VSF in modern photometric surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the Euclid mission.
comments: 13 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Prepared for submission to ApJL

title: Rapid Equation of State Inference from Multiprobe Datasets
authors: Tamal RoyChowdhury, Anarya Ray, Jolien Creighton, Shaon Ghosh
abstract: Fully constraining the neutron star equation of state (EoS) requires combining observations from various channels that probe different density regimes. We perform a joint multimessenger inference of the equation of state using gravitational-wave observations from binary neutron star mergers, NICER mass-radius measurements of X-ray pulsars, and radio timing measurements of massive pulsars. We constrain the parametrized equation of state and perform Bayesian model selection among a set of candidate equations of state. The joint analysis produces a radius of $R_{1.4} = 11.93^{+1.02}_{-0.83} \, \rm km$ for a canonical $1.4 \, M_\odot$ neutron star, and a maximum non-rotating neutron star mass of $M_{\rm max} = 2.31^{+0.23}_{-0.23} \, M_\odot$ with $90\%$ credible intervals. Gravitational-wave and NICER observations constrain the equation of state at low to intermediate densities, while massive pulsar observations constrain it at high densities by requiring the equation of state to support the neutron star masses. We find no simple correlation between the stiffness of an EoS and Bayesian evidence because the observations probe the pressure at different density regimes. By combining constraints on the equation of state with Bayesian model selection using multimessenger data, our analysis connects macroscopic neutron star measurements to microscopic properties of candidate nuclear matter models.
comments: 12 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables

Red error bars show twice the standard deviation of Bayes factors obtained using the bootstrap approach for GW and NICER posterior samples, with corresponding uncertainties propagated to joint analysis. No error bars are shown for the radio only Bayes factors because the likelihood is calculated directly from the mass measurements rather than from a KDE reconstruction. Differences in the Bayes factors obtained from GW, NICER, and radio observations indicate the complementary sensitivity of the different observations to the EoS. See Tab. 4 for the Bayes factors.

title: Discovery of HEC14: an ultra-faint stellar system in M31's outer halo at the globular cluster-dwarf galaxy boundary
authors: Joanna D. Sakowska, David Martínez-Delgado, Massimiliano Gatto, Matteo Monelli, Giuseppe Donatiello, Andrés del Pino, Michelle L. M. Collins, Amandine Doliva-Dolinsky, Ethan D. Taylor
abstract: We present the discovery of HEC14, an ultra-faint stellar system near M31, visually identified in the Pan-Andromeda Archaeological Survey and characterised with deeper OSIRIS+@GTC imaging. HEC14's colour-magnitude diagram shows a clear red giant branch and a well-populated blue horizontal branch, indicating old (>10 Gyr), metal poor stellar populations. We find 912$^{+88}_{-80}$ kpc to be the best-fitting heliocentric distance to the satellite, consistent with M31's outer halo. With $M_{V} \sim -5.00^{+0.51}_{-0.44}$ and a half-light radius of $r_{\rm h} \sim 31^{+13}_{-9}$pc HEC14 lies in the size-luminosity gap between globular clusters and dwarf galaxies. The satellite therefore sits in the extended clusters (EC) regime, making it one of the faintest ECs discovered yet in M31. HEC14 is a new member of M31's halo EC population, whose origins remain unclear two decades after their discovery. We serendipitously find that HEC14's size and luminosity match theoretical predictions for dwarf galaxies with globular cluster-like sizes. Star formation history and/or spectroscopic studies are required to determine whether HEC14 (and possibly all ECs) is genuinely an extended globular cluster or a compact dwarf galaxy.
comments: 9 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Submitted to Astronomy and Astrophysics

title: Deep Multiwavelength Constraints on the Host Galaxies and Black-Hole Growth of Dwarf AGNs
authors: Wei Leong Tee, W. N. Brandt, Zhibo Yu, Fan Zou, Bojun Zhang
abstract: We present a multiwavelength population study of 56 X-ray-detected dwarf galaxies ($M_* < 3 \times 10^9 M_\odot$), comprising 31 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and 25 galaxies (not satisfying AGN classification) in the Chandra Deep Fields North and South. Utilizing ultra-deep Chandra observations together with high-resolution JWST and HST imaging, we investigate the demographics, host-galaxy properties, environments, and cosmic evolution of accreting black holes in low-mass galaxies out to $z\approx4$. We find no statistically significant differences in either the local environments or non-parametric morphologies of X-ray AGNs relative to mass- and redshift-matched inactive dwarf galaxies. These results suggest that AGN activity in dwarf galaxies does not generally require ongoing major mergers or strong large-scale disturbances. Using a single power-law model for the specific accretion-rate distribution, we infer a positive cosmic evolution of dwarf-galaxy black-hole growth. Both the observed AGN fraction and the long-term average black-hole accretion rate increase toward higher redshift and show a positive stellar-mass dependence. Many dwarf AGNs exhibit weak optical and near-infrared AGN signatures, consistent with moderate accretion rates and, at high redshift, potentially enhanced obscuration. The small number of detected systems at $z>2$ limits definitive conclusions, but their hard X-ray colors suggest that obscuration may play an increasingly important role in the dwarf AGN population in the early universe. Our results support a picture in which black-hole growth in dwarf galaxies proceeds through largely stochastic or secular processes while gradually increasing in prevalence toward cosmic noon, providing new empirical constraints on the low-mass end of black hole-galaxy coevolution.
comments: 22+4 pages, 12+1 figures, 1+1 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ

figs.cap: Left: Distribution of X-ray-detected dwarf galaxies in the $L_{\mathrm{X}}-M_{\ast}$ plane. The stellar-mass threshold for dwarf galaxies ($M_{\ast}=3\times 10^{9}~M_{\odot}$) is indicated by the black solid line. Black dashed lines represent the stellar-mass completeness limit for each field, while the orange dashed line indicates the completeness limit for HST. Only mass-complete sources above the black dashed lines are used to derive the star-forming main sequence and for subsequent analyses. The apparent vertical clustering reflects photo-$z$ systematics rather than intrinsic physical overdensities.

The histograms compare the structural properties of X-ray dwarf AGNs (red), X-ray dwarf galaxies (blue), and a mass- and redshift-matched sample of field galaxies (gray, counts are scaled down by a factor of 3 for clarity). The horizontal bars denote the median values and 1$\sigma$ ranges for each respective sample. For comparative context, median values from the recent literature are overlaid in the low-redshift bin: Zhong et al. [115] is represented by green dotted vertical lines, and Tian et al. [96] is represented by magenta markers with error bars. The extensive overlap among the distributions across all four parameters indicates that there is no clear morphological distinction between the active and inactive dwarf galaxies in this sample.

Left, middle, and right panels: Accretion-rate distribution functions in three redshift bins, evaluated at the median $L_{\mathrm{X}}$ of each $M_{\ast}-z$ bin. Two representative stellar masses are shown: $M_{\ast,\mathrm{median}}=10^{7.8}~M_{\odot}$ (dark cyan) and $M_{\ast,\mathrm{median}}=10^{9}~M_{\odot}$ (magenta). Solid curves denote the medians of the posterior sampling distributions, with shaded regions indicating the $1\sigma$ uncertainties derived from the sampling percentiles. Dotted curves represent the results from 116, scaled to the $z$–$M_{\ast}$–$L_{\mathrm{X}}$ coverage of the current sample. Filled circles with error bars represent binned measurements, calculated by incorporating the expected AGN counts given the survey depth and median luminosity in each bin. Constraints are strongest at $z<1$, while only the higher-mass bin ($M_{\ast}\gtrsim 10^{9}~M_{\odot}$) is populated at $z>1$.

Evolution of the AGN fraction ($f_{\mathrm{AGN}}$) as a function of redshift. We compute the AGN fraction by integrating the posterior probability density distributions for sources with $L_{\mathrm{X}}=10^{40}$–$10^{43}~\mathrm{erg~s^{-1}}$. The mass dependence is illustrated by the dark cyan ($M_{\ast}=10^{7.8}~M_{\odot}$) and magenta ($M_{\ast}=10^{9}~M_{\odot}$) solid curves, with the shaded regions indicating the $1\sigma$ uncertainties. These curves are truncated at higher redshifts where the respective stellar mass falls below our observational mass completeness limit (as shown in Figure 3), ensuring that the plotted fractions rely on robust measurements. For comparison, we overplot observational constraints from several $z<1$ dwarf AGN studies, color-coded to correspond to our adopted stellar-mass bins. Where necessary, the literature values are derived by summing the contributions across all available luminosity bins. The comparison sample includes Reines et al. [81] (downward triangles), Pardo et al. [75] (gray shaded region), Aird et al. [1] (squares), Mezcua et al. [64] (circles), Birchall et al. [6] (diamonds), and 116 (dotted curves). A broken $x$-axis is employed to expand the low-redshift ($z\leq 1$) regime for clearer visualization of the literature constraints, while the $z>1$ range is compressed.

Evolution of the $\overline{\mathrm{BHAR}}$ as a function of redshift for different stellar-mass regimes. The solid dark-cyan ($M_{\ast}=10^{7.8}~M_{\odot}$) and magenta ($M_{\ast}=10^{9}~M_{\odot}$) curves show the joint dwarf-galaxy estimates obtained by combining the X-ray dwarf AGNs in this work with the dwarf AGNs from 116. These curves represent the observed dwarf-AGN contribution at $L_{\mathrm{X}}=10^{40}$–$10^{44}~\mathrm{erg~s^{-1}}$, and the shaded regions indicate the $1\sigma$ uncertainty around the median. The dash-dotted curves show the empirically corrected dwarf-galaxy estimates, where a redshift-dependent fractional correction is applied to account for the possible contribution from the unobserved high-luminosity tail at $L_{\rm X}>10^{44}~\mathrm{erg~s^{-1}}$. The correction is calibrated from the ratio between the $\overline{\mathrm{BHAR}}$ predicted by the Zou et al. [118] relation over $L_{\rm X}=10^{44}$–$10^{46}~\mathrm{erg~s^{-1}}$ and that over $L_{\rm X}=10^{41}$–$10^{44}~\mathrm{erg~s^{-1}}$, evaluated at $M_{\ast,\rm ref}=10^{9.75}~M_{\odot}$. For comparison, the dotted orange and purple curves show the massive-galaxy relations from Zou et al. [118] for $M_{\ast}=10^{10.5}~M_{\odot}$ and $M_{\ast}=10^{9.75}~M_{\odot}$, respectively, integrated over $L_{\mathrm{X}}=10^{41}$–$10^{46}~\mathrm{erg~s^{-1}}$.

title: Infrared spectrum of the Type Iax supernova remnant Pa30
authors: D. P. K. Banerjee, A. Evans, S. Starrfield, C. E. Woodward, T. R. Geballe, V. Joshi, D. J. Hillier, L. Izzo, M. Della Valle, G. Shaw, G. Rangwal, S. Sharma
abstract: The central star of Pa30 and its nebulosity offer one of the best opportunities to study a SN Iax explosion and its remnant. Pa30 is thought to be the product of the historical supernova explosion of 1181. No infrared spectroscopy of its extremely hot central star has hitherto been reported. Here, we present a 0.75-5 $\mu$m spectrum taken by the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), together with ground-based infrared spectra, at higher resolution, covering the 0.8-2.5 $\mu$m region. The spectra contain very broad lines, which we have attempted to identify and model using the codes CMFGEN and CLOUDY. The CMFGEN modelling suggests that most of the lines are due to OVI. However, CLOUDY modelling, using expected theoretical abundances for the bound remnants of SN Iax explosions, provides evidence for the presence of coronal lines of Si, S, Mg, and Al arising from a shocked gas. This strengthens the suggestion that Pa30 is indeed the remnant of a SN Iax explosion.
comments: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 8 pages, 4 figures

title: The GECKOS Survey: deriving bar properties in edge-on galaxies from molecular gas kinematics
authors: A. Fraser-McKelvie, T. A. Davis, M. Bureau, R. Cai, S. M. Croom, Y. Ding, E. Emsellem, F. Fragkoudi, M. Frosst, D. A. Gadotti, O. Gerhard, E. J. Iles, G. Krahm, R. Leaman, M. Martig, B. Mazzilli Ciraulo, I. Minchev, F. Pinna, A. Poci, C. de Sá-Freitas, L. Valenzuela, J. van de Sande, G. van de Ven, Z. Wang, T. Zafar, L. Zhu
abstract: The characterisation of disc-connected structures such as bars and nuclear rings is a difficult task in edge-on galaxies. We present a simple method to derive bar position angles and lengths in edge-on galaxies using molecular gas kinematics from ALMA observations. Our approach exploits the geometry of bar-driven gas flows: assuming that cold molecular gas settles into an elliptical nuclear ring oriented orthogonally to the bar, the line-of-sight velocity of the nuclear ring varies predictably with bar viewing angle. Using only the observed nuclear ring velocity and a circular velocity derived from Multi-Gaussian Expansion (MGE) stellar mass models, we construct a grid of bisymmetric bar flow models spanning a range of radial and transverse velocities to constrain the bar position angle. We validate this methodology on a toy model and an isolated galaxy hydrodynamical simulation snapshot, demonstrating that the technique reliably distinguishes three viewing angle brackets: side-on (0° - 35°), intermediate (35° - 65°), and end-on (65° - 90°). Applying this method to six GECKOS Survey galaxies hosting boxy-peanut bulges with ALMA CO observations, we find four bars oriented side-on, one at an intermediate angle, and one end-on case (IC 1711), the latter confirming predictions from stellar kinematics alone. Derived nuclear ring sizes and deprojected bar lengths are broadly consistent with measurements from more face-on literature samples. This method offers a practical and computationally inexpensive means of constraining bar properties in edge-on galaxies, complementing full dynamical modelling approaches.
comments: 11 pages, 6 figures (+4 appendix pages and 7 appendix figures). Submitted to A&A

figs.cap: Toy model of a bar (grey) embedded within a gas disc (purple) that formed a nuclear disc (white; elongated for illustrative purposes) and a nuclear ring located at the outer edge of the nuclear disc (purple). The snapshots (top) show the same model with three different bar position angles, with $0\degr$ being side-on and $90\degr$ end-on. For each bar orientation, the gas PVD of the galaxy when seen edge-on (i.e. along the y-axis) is shown beneath. If we assume that the bar-built nuclear gas ring is ellipsoidal and with a position angle perpendicular to that of the bar, clear differences are seen in the maximal velocity of the nuclear ring region in the resultant PVDs (located at an x offset of 0), resulting from the changing projected geometry of the nuclear ring.

Top: face-on projection of the gas mass volume density, $\rho$, of the RAMSES run of an isolated, Milky Way-like barred disc galaxy (Fragkoudi & Bieri, in prep.). The bar is at a position angle of 155$\degr$, and the final, $3.3$ Gyr snapshot is shown. Bottom: the resultant PVD extracted with KinMS when the galaxy is viewed edge-on.

Determination of the bar viewing angle $\theta_{\rm bar}$ from the set of model lines generated from mock ALMA cubes by KinMS. The four lines of each colour show different $V_{t}$ values, and the relative transparency corresponds to the different $V_{r}$ values for the given $V_{t}$. The three grey horizontal shaded regions denote three measurements of $V_{\rm{NR}}$ from the PVD for three different bar position angles, $\theta_{\rm bar}=$ $0\degr$, $50\degr$ and $90\degr$. The $\theta_{\rm bar}$ range over which the model lines intersect a measured $V_{\rm{NR}}$ corresponds to the range of possible bar viewing angles. For a given input $V_{\rm{NR}}$, we see that the technique recovers the actual position angle well.

Violin plots showing the distribution of recovered bar position angles ($\theta_{\rm bar,est}$) for each model for a given input angle ($\theta_{\rm b}$), inferred from $V_{\rm{NR}}$. The purple violins are derived using the toy models, yellow using the hydrodynamical simulation snapshot. In both cases, the median of the distribution is indicated by the horizontal lines. The red $1:1$ line indicates good overall agreement between the recovered and true bar position angles. There are clear differences in parameter space covered between the $\theta_{\rm bar,est}$ distributions at small, intermediate and large bar position angles, from which we conclude that we can confidently differentiate only three brackets of bar viewing angles, labelled here as side-on, intermediate and end-on.

Derivation of the bar position angles of six GECKOS survey galaxies. For each galaxy, $16$ different model predictions of the nuclear ring line-of-sight velocity $V_{\rm{NR}}$ are plotted in the bottom panel as a function of the bar position angle $\theta_{\rm bar}$, given the galaxy circular velocity curve and combinations of radial and transverse velocities $(V_{r},V_{t})$. The grey horizontal band denotes the measurement of $V_{\rm obs}(R_{\rm NR}$) derived from the ALMA PVD, including a $10$ km s$^{-1}$ uncertainty (the data cubes’ channel width). The region in which the model curves intersect the grey band corresponds to the range of possible bar position angles allowed by the models. This range is converted to a probability, illustrated by the grey horizontal violin plot in the top panel. The median of the probability distributuion is marked by a white bar. The predicted bar position angle is then defined as the one of three pre-defined position angle brackets which overlaps most with the violin plot, shown as a purple shaded region.

Comparison of the derived (deprojected) bar radii and (projected) nuclear ring radii of the GECKOS ALMA sample galaxies (crosses) to those of Erwin (2024; orange squares) and the nuclear stellar discs of de Sá-Freitas et al. (2025; red squares). Our measurements are plotted at the mid range of the position angle brackets, except for IC 1711, where we plot the lower limit. When visible, error bars denote the bar lengths calculated at the edges of the position angle brackets. Despite the large uncertainties introduced by large bar position angles, the derived bar lengths are broadly consistent with those measured from the literature measures reported for face-on galaxies. Note: the bar radii plotted here are half of the deprojected bar lengths listed in Table 1.

title: Asteroseismology of AI Velorum: a prototype of high-amplitude delta Scuti stars
authors: Przemysław Walczak, Jadwiga Daszyńska-Daszkiewicz, Wojciech Niewiadomski, Wojciech Szewczuk
abstract: AI Velorum is exceptional among high-amplitude \delta Scuti (HADS) stars because of its multimode pulsations. Despite being an excellent target for asteroseismology, this prototype star has not been studied in detail. We determine the stellar parameters, age, and evolutionary stage of AI Vel, constrain envelope convection and convective core overshooting, and test three opacity data sets: OPAL, OP, and OPLIB. We analysed TESS photometry, ground-based Strömgren photometry, and HARPS spectroscopy. Modes were identified using photometric and spectroscopic methods, and empirical values of the non-adiabatic f-parameter were derived for both radial modes. Seismic modelling was performed within a Bayesian framework supported by Monte Carlo simulations. We confirm the radial nature of the two dominant modes and identify one non-radial mode as most likely an axisymmetric dipole or quadrupole mode. Within the explored parameter space, only OPAL models reproduce the observed position of AI Vel in the HR diagram, whereas OP and OPLIB models are too cool and underluminous. All seismic models favour inefficient envelope convection (mixing-length parameter alpha_{mlt}\lesssim 0.5). Including the non-radial mode substantially reduces the formal posterior uncertainties, but the ambiguity in its identification introduces additional model-dependent uncertainties. AI Vel is an evolved, slowly rotating star in the hydrogen shell-burning phase. Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combining pulsation frequencies with empirical f-parameters. The preference for OPAL opacities is consistent with results for several other HADS and SX Phoenicis stars but does not imply a general superiority of OPAL opacities.
comments: 15 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: Cross-Dataset Inference of Central-Satellite Classification and Host Halo Masses from Galaxy neighbours with Machine Learning
authors: Alice Chen, Camille Avestruz, Niayesh Afshordi, Yen-Ting Lin
abstract: The classification of galaxies as centrals or satellites gives insight into the galaxy-halo connection. This, together with halo mass estimates, can be used to connect observed galaxy populations to underlying dark matter structure. To (1) classify galaxies as centrals or satellites and (2) estimate the host halo mass for centrals, we train XGBoost models on IllustrisTNG (TNG100) galaxies, using the distances (3D or projected (2+1)D redshift space) and $M_*$ of their ten nearest neighbours. We then test the model on EAGLE to measure its robustness after applying a simple domain-alignment step that corrects for a relative shift in the $M_*$ distribution between TNG100 and EAGLE. We further augment the training data by combining feature sets from neighbour samples with varying lower $M_*$ thresholds. On the TNG100 test set, the central/satellite classifier reaches purity and completeness $=0.97$ (0.95) in 3D (projected redshift) space at the threshold where purity=completeness, and the halo-mass regressor achieves $r^2$=0.98 (0.93) when evaluated on true centrals and $r^2=0.93$ (0.93) when evaluated on inferred centrals. Applied to EAGLE after alignment, the classifier achieves purity/completeness $=0.95$ (0.95), while halo-mass inference yields $r^2=0.91$ ($0.87$) for true centrals and $r^2=0.83$ (0.77) for inferred centrals; training-data augmentation most improves the halo-mass estimation task. Satellites misclassified as centrals underpredict the true masses of host halos, especially if they are closer to a lower mass halo's central than its own host's central and/or has a significantly lower $M_*$ than its own central. These results show that survey-accessible information such as projected separations and stellar masses - combined with simulation-trained models and domain alignment - can enable reliable central identification and host halo mass estimation to an $r^2\geq 0.85$.
comments: 15 pages, 16 Figures (including appendix), comments are welcome
