title: Potential spectral markers of intrinsic magnetic fields of hot exoplanets in the UV range
authors: M. Rumenskikh, S. S. Sharipov, I. F. Shaikhislamov, A. E. Ivanova, M. P. Golubovsky, K. S. Shcherbakov, A. V. Taichenachev, L. A. Maksimova
abstract: A method for detecting the intrinsic magnetic fields of exoplanets, based on the effect of atomic alignment (the redistribution of populations among magnetic sublevels under the action of anisotropic radiation from the host star), has been adapted for observations with the Spektr-UV space telescope. A procedure for selecting sensitive transitions is proposed, and triplet absorption lines in the UV range that are sensitive to alignment are identified. On the basis of three-dimensional aeronomic models of the hot Jupiters KELT-20 b and HAT-P-32 b, absorption spectra in these lines are calculated for cases with and without intrinsic magnetic fields of the exoplanets. Using the Spektr-UV exposure-time calculator, the observability of the effect is assessed, and an observing program is proposed, specifying the optimal duration of individual exposures and the number of transits required to detect the signal.

title: A Homogeneous Benchmark of Exoplanet Mass-Radius Relations
authors: Ailar Alizadehsabegh, Soroush Sarabi, Atila Poro
abstract: The mass-radius ($M$-$R$) relation is fundamental to inferring the bulk composition and internal structure of exoplanets. However, published relations remain difficult to compare directly because studies adopt different planetary samples, fitting procedures, and evaluation metrics. We construct a homogeneous, quality-controlled benchmark of 963 exoplanets with dynamically measured masses and transit radii from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. We compare empirical power laws, probabilistic models, and machine-learning (ML) regressors using point accuracy, interval coverage, and probabilistic calibration. On the full test set, a multi-feature random forest has the lowest root-mean-square error, 0.329~dex in $\log_{10} M$ versus 0.368~dex for a fitted two-parameter power law ($p = 0.007$ unadjusted; $p = 0.059$ after Holm correction across 13 comparisons). Radius-only ML models perform comparably to the single power law. In three ranges of the measured radius, several methods improve on the power law below 1.6 $R_\oplus$, but none does between 1.6 and 4 $R_\oplus$. Including stellar and orbital covariates significantly improves predictions only for low-mass planets ($M < 4.4\,M_\oplus$), although this result is sensitive to missing covariate data and weakens when the training and test sets are separated by host star. Within their calibrated radius domains, the published empirical and probabilistic relations remain highly competitive. Finally, a first-order variance decomposition shows that formal measurement uncertainties account for only $\sim$3\% of the residual variance (0.067 of 0.401~dex), and the remaining $\sim$0.396~dex arises from compositional diversity, selection effects, and model approximation error.
comments: Accepted by the Astrophysics Journal

title: Deconstructing the cosmic baryon distribution with fast radio bursts
authors: Koustav Konar, Yin-Zhe Ma, Léon V. E. Koopmans, P. Daniel Meerburg
abstract: The precise distribution of baryons in the Universe remains an open question in cosmology, as their highly diffuse nature hinders direct observation. However, mapping it is integral for precision cosmology in studies of gravitational lensing, galaxy evolution and the cosmic microwave background with current and upcoming surveys. We use fast radio bursts (FRBs) and their dispersion measures (DMs) to probe and localise this baryon distribution in the large-scale structure (LSS). Using IllustrisTNG simulations, we classify the LSS into eight bins of increasing matter density, analogous to voids, filaments, and haloes. We model the DM contribution from each substructure and compare it with the simulated DMs to infer the density estimator, the ratio of electron number to total matter density. The resulting overdetermined system is solved in a Bayesian framework with a simulation-physics-informed model. To demonstrate observational applicability, we create a Euclid-like mock galaxy catalogue and build a density estimator based on luminous matter along FRB sightlines. We apply a bias correction for the underlying dark matter distribution and compare the two density estimators to recover the electron number density across the eight bins. Electrons are predominantly localised in low-density regions, while the ensemble mean across all bins aligns with the global theoretical estimate. Combining the FRB and galaxy density estimators, we recover the density of ionised baryons as $\Omega_b f_{ion} = 0.0455^{+0.0028}_{-0.0026}$ (simulation: 0.0462), corresponding to $\Omega_b = 0.0479^{+0.0029}_{-0.0027}$ for $f_{ion}=0.95$. Our bin-wise electron density estimate reproduces the simulation ground truth to within 10 per cent and gives gas fractions of $0.186 \pm 0.012$, $0.179 \pm 0.015$ and $0.046 \pm 0.014$ in voids, filaments and haloes, against ground truths of 0.167, 0.173 and 0.067.
comments: Accepted for publication in A&A

title: Discovery of a Massive Outer Companion to the TOI-178 Resonant Chain
authors: Emma V. Turtelboom, William Thompson, Ryan Cloutier, Alexandra Rochon, Charles A. Beichman, Trevor Campbell, Nick Choksi, Doug Johnstone, Jessica Speedie, Dori Blakely, Simon Blouin, Alexandre Bouchard-Côté, Brendan P. Bowler, David R. Ciardi, Clarissa R. Do Ó, Andre Fogal, Kyle Franson, Kaitlyn Hessel, Christian Marois, Eric Nielsen, William Roberson, Jean-Baptiste Ruffio, Judah Van Zandt, Jerry W. Xuan, Jingwen Zhang
abstract: We report the discovery of a massive outer companion around TOI-178, a known planetary system with six inner small planets within 0.15 AU, five of which are in a 2:4:6:9:12 resonant chain. We analyse the astrometric anomalies in the combined Gaia DR2/DR3 - Hipparcos catalogue (G23H) and literature radial velocities, revealing strong evidence for a massive outer companion at several AU. We combine the resulting orbital fit posterior with archival high-contrast imaging to constrain the properties of the corresponding massive outer companion, TOI-178 h. We also study the dynamical stability of the inner resonant chain in the presence of this previously unknown outer companion via both heuristic and N-body simulations. We find that the inner system appears to be robust to the perturbing influence of TOI-178\,h, in line with the systems several Gyr age. Our analysis results in a final posterior solution for TOI-178\,h with a semi-major axis of $6.9^{+12.3}_{-3.3}$ AU, a mass of $21^{+47}_{-11} M_J$, and eccentricity of $0.76^{+0.18}_{-0.35}$, likely corresponding to an eccentric brown dwarf. TOI-178 is currently the only known system that has maintained a high-multiplicity resonant chain whilst in the dynamical presence of a massive outer companion, showcasing a unique outcome of planet formation.
comments: Submitted to PASP

title: Bar formation and secular evolution in live Milky Way-like galaxies
authors: Eva Durán-Camacho, Sioree Ansar, Paula D. López, Johan H. Knapen, Jesus Falcón-Barroso, Adriana de Lorenzo-Cáceres, Jairo Méndez-Abreu
abstract: Context. Bars and their boxy/peanut (B/P) shapes drive the secular evolution of disc galaxies, redistributing angular momentum and reshaping the radial and vertical structure of stellar discs. Bars occur in bulgeless to bulge-dominated hosts. Bars are known to grow and slow down, but how this relates to host galaxy structure remains poorly understood. Aims. We investigate how the formation and evolution of bars and B/P structures depend on the initial stellar mass and bulge fraction of Milky Way (MW)-like galaxies, and explore the links between disc kinematic settling, bar formation, resonance structure, and vertical thickening. Methods. We analyse fifteen isolated MW-like hydrodynamical simulations run with AREPO for 3 Gyr, spanning three stellar masses and five bulge fractions, with live stellar, bulge, and dark matter components. We measure bar properties via Fourier decomposition, locate resonances from circular and epicyclic frequencies, and quantify B/P evolution from the vertical stellar distribution. Results. Bar formation timing depends strongly on galaxy structure. Low-mass galaxies generally form bars only after global disc kinematics have settled, whereas the most massive systems can form bars while the orbital distribution is still evolving. All bars slow down and grow in strength and size, and remain in the slow-bar regime. B/P structures form shortly after the bar and keep growing, appearing much earlier in more massive and disc-dominated galaxies. Only one model shows a clear buckling event; the rest form B/P bulges through smooth secular evolution. Conclusions. Initial stellar mass and bulge fraction strongly regulate the timing of bar and B/P formation. We find a coherent evolutionary sequence linking bar growth, bar slowdown, and B/P assembly, whose timing is set by the initial disc structure rather than by its global kinematic settling.
comments: 15 pages, 11 figures, accepted on A&A

title: New Observational Insights into Generalised Axion-Like Dark Energy
authors: Mariam Bouhmadi-López, Hsu-Wen Chiang, Carlos G. Boiza, Thomas J. Broadhust
abstract: We consider a quintessence model based on a generalised axion-like scalar field potential, originally introduced as a phenomenological framework to describe the late-time accelerated expansion of the Universe. The model exhibits a tracking regime that alleviates the coincidence problem and naturally leads to a phase of late-time acceleration driven by an effective cosmological constant, without requiring fine-tuning of the scalar field initial conditions. In this work, we confront the background cosmological evolution of this model with current observations by performing a parameter inference analysis using cosmic microwave background distance priors, baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, Type Ia supernovae, the SH0ES distance ladder, cosmic chronometers, and gamma-ray bursts. This analysis allows us to assess the observational viability of the model, its ability to reconcile different cosmological datasets, and its statistical performance relative to $\Lambda$CDM.
comments: 23 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables, RevTex 4-2

figs.cap: Compactified generalised axion-like potential $V(\phi)/\Lambda^{4}=[1-\cos(\phi/f)]^{-n}$ as a function of $\phi/f$ over one period, for representative values of $n$. The vertical axis uses the compactified mapping $\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan\!\big(V/\Lambda^{4}\big)$, which renders the divergences at $\phi/f=0$ and $2\pi$ finite while preserving the minimum at $\phi/f=\pi$. Dashed curves show the quadratic expansion around the minimum, $V/\Lambda^{4}\simeq 2^{-n}+\frac{n}{4}2^{-n}(\phi/f-\pi)^{2}$.

Representative background evolution of the generalised axion-like quintessence model for $n=1$. Panel (a) tests the dependence on the initial scalar field displacement by varying $\phi_{\rm ini}/f$ while keeping the values of $n$ and $f$ fixed within each branch. The different trajectories exhibit the expected tracking behaviour, approaching $w_{\phi}\simeq-1/2$ during matter domination for $n=1$, and later evolving toward the same asymptotic de Sitter solution with $w_{\phi}\to-1$. Panels (b) and (c) compare two late-time regimes: a non-oscillatory case with $f=1\,M_{\rm Pl}$ and an oscillatory case with $f=0.1\,M_{\rm Pl}$, both evolved from $\phi_{\rm ini}/f=10^{-4}$ and $\dot{\phi}_{\rm ini}=0$. Panel (b) shows the radiation, matter and scalar field density parameters, while panel (c) shows their residuals with respect to the $\Lambda$CDM reference. The comparison shows that the value of $f$ controls the late-time approach to the minimum of the potential, distinguishing oscillatory from overdamped evolution, whereas the tracker reduces the sensitivity to the initial value of the scalar field.

title: LEMUR: A Searchable Web Archive of Deep Chandra Images of Galaxies and Galaxy Clusters
authors: Carter L. Rhea, Julie Hlavacek-Larrondo, Marine Prunier, Hyunseop Choi, Megan Donahue, Christian Thibeault
abstract: We present LEMUR, a publicly accessible archive of uniformly reduced, deep Chandra images of 2,569 galaxies and galaxy clusters (including groups), comprising 5,505 ACIS observations and 138.8 Ms of exposure. By combining the publicly available imaging observations of each target, we provide background-subtracted, exposure-corrected images in broad, soft, and hard bands at the native ACIS pixel scale of 0.492 arcsec. Our primary goal is to make the wealth of archival Chandra observations accessible to researchers without requiring specialized expertise in X-ray data reduction. Each observation is reprocessed with CIAO, filtered for background flares, and reduced with settings chosen to preserve faint diffuse emission; the merged images are exposure corrected and background subtracted using the ACIS blank-sky backgrounds in a broad (0.5-7.0 keV), a soft (0.5-2.0 keV), and a hard (2.0-7.0 keV) band. For every object, we measure an X-ray center at the peak of its diffuse emission, and we provide a morphological similarity search based on embeddings from the AstroCLIP foundation model, in which nearest neighbors share cool-core status in 73% of matched cluster pairs, compared with 51% by chance. Photometry of 275 point sources agrees with the Chandra Source Catalog to within 3% in the broad band. The images, along with their counts images, background models, exposure maps, and quick-look stamps, are available through a searchable web archive at this https URL. The catalog tables are archived on Zenodo (doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24351915), and all code is open source at this https URL.
comments: Will be submitting to the Open Journal of Astrophysics

title: Map-Level Inference of Primordial Gravitational Waves from the CMB with Spherical Neural Networks
authors: Anto I. Lonappan, Adrian E. Bayer, Brian Keating, Kam Arnold, Giuseppe Puglisi, Ethan O. Nadler
abstract: We train a spherical graph convolutional network to infer the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ directly from multifrequency cosmic microwave background (CMB) $B$-mode maps on the cut sky. We test the network on simulations of a generic ground-based experiment including lensed CMB, inhomogeneous noise, and stochastic Galactic dust and synchrotron emission. We compare the network with a multifrequency bandpower likelihood built from the same 20,000 simulations used to train it. Working directly on the maps, with no power-spectrum estimation or component separation, the network reduces the root-mean-square error on $r$ by a factor of 1.3 and gives well-calibrated 68% intervals 1.2 times narrower than the likelihood with the same prior. Saliency maps show that the network learns to favor the deepest regions of the sky and the cleanest frequency channels without being given the survey depth. Both approaches are tied to the foreground model they are built on: the network generalizes to some alternative foreground models without retraining, but not to a three-dimensional dust model with line-of-sight variations. The network can be extended to marginalize over foreground models by training on a broad family, making direct map-level neural inference a promising route to $r$ for future $B$-mode analyses.
comments: 15 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables
